articles.title: Samsung actualiza por error sus frigoríficos y los deja inservibles
articles.text:
Comprar un electrodoméstico inteligente podría ser la peor decisión que hayas tomado, sobre todo si dependes de su funcionamiento. Para muestra basta lo que ocurrió en Corea del Sur, cuando Samsung lanzó por error una actualización de software para sus frigoríficos que todavía estaba en fase de pruebas. Esto provocó que los dispositivos dejaran de funcionar, provocando que la comida se echara a perder en vísperas de una festividad clave en ese país.
Decenas de propietarios de frigoríficos Family Hub reportaron en los foros oficiales de Samsung que sus equipos dejaron de funcionar tras recibir una actualización de SmartThings. De acuerdo con SamMobile, algunos afectados señalaron que se fueron a trabajar con el frigorífico funcionando y al volver se encontraron con que estaba apagado, sin posibilidad de reiniciarlo ni de volver a vincularlo. Si tienes un televisor o barra de sonido Samsung compatible con SmartThings, estarás al tanto de este fallo que no se resuelve al eliminar e intentar vincular de nuevo.
Además de los frigoríficos apagados, otros usuarios describieron que la apertura automática de la puerta dejó de funcionar o que la luz interior ya no encendía. Samsung reconoció el incidente y explicó que se debió a que publicaron por error una versión del software que todavía se encontraba en fase de pruebas. El fabricante detuvo el despliegue de la actualización y envió a sus técnicos a reparar los equipos afectados para tenerlos funcionando lo antes posible.
La crisis de los frigoríficos no pudo llegar en un peor momento. Este jueves 24 de septiembre se celebra el Chuseok, una de las festividades más importantes de Corea del Sur, donde la comida ocupa un lugar primordial en las reuniones familiares. Samsung prometió a los usuarios que resolvería el problema antes de esa fecha.
¿Por qué los frigoríficos de Samsung dependen tanto del software?
El fallo de los frigoríficos Family Hub ha expuesto el talón de Aquiles de los electrodomésticos inteligentes. Si bien gran parte de las preocupaciones del hogar inteligente y los dispositivos IoT suele centrarse en la seguridad, la dependencia del software también es algo para tomar en cuenta.
En el caso de los frigoríficos de Samsung, el equipo depende de que el software funcione correctamente para cumplir tareas tan elementales como mantenerse frío. Estos dispositivos están pensados para integrarse por completo con el ecosistema SmartThings, por lo que incorporan cámaras internas que identifican los alimentos y permiten consultar el interior desde el móvil. En caso de que algún producto esté a punto de agotarse o de caducar, el sistema te enviará una notificación.
Además de la gestión de alimentos, los frigoríficos inteligentes actúan como centro de control del hogar. Desde su pantalla se pueden manejar otros componentes de Smart Things y soportan comandos de voz mediante Bixby. Los usuarios pueden aprovechar para duplicar la pantalla del móvil o del televisor y mirar una serie o vídeo de YouTube mientras cocinan.
Todo suena muy bien, pero este nivel de conectividad tiene una debilidad y es que, cuantas más funciones están ligadas al software, mayores son las probabilidades de que algo salga mal. En un escenario como el de la actualización fallida de Samsung, los propietarios se quedan con un frigorífico que ni siquiera puede mantener operando sus funciones básicas. En el peor de los casos, un modelo que ya no tenga soporte ni actualizaciones quedaría inservible y obligaría al usuario a gastar dinero para comprar uno nuevo.

articles.title: $14,000 gaming PC features 70 handcrafted titanium cherry blossoms which unfurl as temperatures rise — Zotac-designed RTX 5080 system features impressive sculpture and an eye-watering price tag to match
articles.text:
$14,000 gaming PC features 70 handcrafted titanium cherry blossoms which unfurl as temperatures rise — Zotac-designed RTX 5080 system features impressive sculpture and an eye-watering price tag to match
Cherry blossoms open and close using heat generated by the system
Forget RGB, OLED screens, figurines, and dioramas. We've never seen anything like the Cherry Bloom PC from Aftershock PC in Australia, though. This liquid-cooled, high-end gaming PC includes a Cherry Blossom tree, featuring 70 handcrafted, heat-reactive titanium-alloy cherry blossoms that unfurl when the machine heats up.
What makes this even more remarkable is that the PC — heat-reactive blossoms included — is actually commercially available, and isn't a one-off custom mod. You can buy one from Aftershock PC right now. There are no motors to break; the blooming blossoms are completely 'powered' by the heat generated from the high-end components in the PC, too. Those components include an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D processor, 64GB of fast DDR5 memory, a 1300-watt modular power supply, and most notably, a GeForce RTX 5080 graphics card.
The presence of an RTX 5080 might be surprising considering the price we mentioned in the headline; yes, this PC costs approximately $14,150 USD ($20,000 AUD, or around £10,650 GBP). But if you've got the cash to spare and are eyeing the PC up, just note that the eye-watering price doesn't include shipping. At that price, it's fair to expect truly top-end components, like a Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 Dual Edition and a GeForce RTX 5090 (as found in the very best PCs for gaming), but honestly, this machine is as much a work of art as a functional PC. You're not merely paying for the components; you're paying for the brilliant display inside.
The chassis used for the Cherry Bloom is the "V2" by Taiwan's Advanced Performance Nexus, better known as APNX. The case has what APNX calls "one of the largest viewing area in its class," with wrap-around glass on three sides to allow you to admire the gorgeous sculpture in your case. Along with the previously mentioned components, you also get a 2TB Lexar NQ790 PCIe 4.0 SSD, a custom open-loop liquid cooling setup, eight Aftershock Chrome RGB fans, and Windows 11 Professional, naturally.
Obviously, the Cherry Bloom PC isn't something that many people are going to buy. Much like the KFC console before it, it's a curious piece of marketing from Zotac Gaming, which designed the PC, according to the product listing. Nevertheless, the mechanism is indeed mind-bending enough. You can check out Aftershock's website and click through the slideshow to view videos showcasing the petals of the 'tree' unfurling; if nothing else, it's impressive to see the mechanism working in motion.

articles.title: 'I'll have to throw away all the holiday food I bought': A Samsung update has broken lots of smart AI fridges in South Korea, including stopping them from cooling — and it's enough to make you question the idea of smart fridges
articles.text:
The problem with smart appliances: some of Samsung's AI fridges have shut down and lost their cool after a bad update was accidentally pushed to them
And right before a national holiday too
- Samsung AI fridges are failing in South Korea ahead of a national holiday
- It doesn't just shut down the smart display, it stops them from keeping things cold
- A broken SmartThings update appears to be to blame, and engineers will visit affected customers to apply the necessary fix
There is a case to be made against stuffing AI and smart tech into every single gadget: case in point, units from Samsung's smart fridge series, which have started shutting down and leaving food uncooled in South Korea after a bad software update was pushed out.
As Notebookcheck reports, this has left users very angry — and right before the Chuseok national holiday too. A host of fridge owners are saying that after an update in SmartThings, their appliances almost immediately stopped working. No interior light, no touch pad functionality, and no refrigeration.
It looks as though the Bespoke AI 4-Door Refrigerator model is the one most affected by the serious glitch, and according to ZDNET Korea, an internal testing software version was rolled out by mistake. Samsung has acknowledged the error, paused the update, and is promising to send out engineers over the holiday break.
However, users are reporting they're only able to book engineers for after Chuseok ends, on Saturday, September 26. "Now it looks like I'll have to throw away all the holiday food I bought ahead of the break," said one disgruntled user (via Google Translate), as per SBS News in South Korea.
Turn it off and on again
Samsung isn't sharing details of how many people have been affected by this, but considering the volume of complaints, it seems to be a significant number. As yet, there's been no mention of any compensation for the fridge contents that will be spoiled — and there doesn't seem to be a fix other than to wait for an engineer.
The unfortunate fridge owners who've been hit by the bug have been resorting to dry ice and ice boxes to try and keep their food and drink cool, but all efforts to roll back the update have proved unsuccessful. Turning the fridges off and on again doesn't work, and nor does removing and reinstating them on the SmartThings platform.
It does seem as though the update was halted before it reached any Samsung fridge customers outside of South Korea, which is good news — but not much consolation for those who are affected. Losing a few smart functions is one thing, but to have the units completely shut down is… well, it's enough to make you rethink the idea of a smart major appliance.

articles.title: Toronto startup SmartARM uses Meta AI glasses to help 'see' objects
articles.text:
Toronto-based robotics startup SmartArm is using AI hardware to help its prosthetic arm grab objects more easily.
SmartArm, which gained recognition for winning Microsoft’s Imagine Cup in 2018, uses self-built AI software and hardware from Meta to let the limb “see” the object and adjust to make grabbing it easier.
It does this using an onboard camera built into the palm that streams video to the operating system, which SmartARM calls Dexterity OS. It identifies the object and automatically selects the optimal grip. From there, the multi-articulating fingers move to grab the object, applying the right pressure for each individual object.
The SmartARM also uses three pieces of Meta technology: the Meta AI glasses, the DINOv2 open-source vision model, and the Meta Wearables Device Access Toolkit. SmartARM’s founder, Hamayal Choudry, noted that the Meta AI glasses let the arm see more of its environment than the palm camera alone. With DINOv2, users can train new objects by taking a few photos in the SmartARM app, and the software identifies similarities and determines the best grip. This means that it allows the arm to grip and pick up objects based directly on visual feature reading, and without needing prior understanding or traditional programming.
The toolkit allows SmartARM to extend and improve object recognition and understanding, which will provide more data from the egocentric point of view that the glasses offer. According to SmartARM’s website, the device currently recognizes over 365 everyday objects, with the library “constantly growing” through over-the-air updates. SmartARM also notes that the more you use the arm, the more objects get added to your personal recognition profile.
Although no device specs are listed yet, SmartARM notes an expected battery life of 12-16 hours, depending on activity level.
Pricing also hasn’t been released, but the company is actively working with insurers and health systems to establish coverage options. The device is currently in beta in Canada, and if you want one, you can join the company’s waitlist for updates and early access to pricing, specs, and more.

articles.title: Modal Motors is trying to cut China out of electric motors entirely | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Lately, it seems like everyone is talking about bringing manufacturing back to the United States, especially when it comes to hard tech like drones and robotics. Michael Van Steenburg thinks he’s ahead of the game.
Van Steenburg spent the last decade building all kinds of electric motors in the U.S. and North America, and now he wants to do it again with his new startup, Modal Motors. This time, he wants to ditch rare-earth magnets entirely, in a bid to further separate the U.S. from China’s supply chain.
As one of the founders in Startup Battlefield 200 who will compete at TechCrunch Disrupt next month, he thinks it’s an urgent pitch to make.
“China’s already flexed its muscles a couple times,” Van Steenburg said, referring to the country restricting access to rare-earth products.
There are other companies working on setting up electric motor manufacturing and supply chains in the U.S., but Van Steenburg argues they’re doing it the wrong way by continuing to rely on rare-earth magnets. Domestic supply of those materials is still years away, he said.
“Other people are ‘reshoring,’ [but] they’re basically knocking off Chinese motors and just doing it in the U.S. But they’re hoping that the U.S. rare-earth magnet system is going to get up to speed fast enough,” he said. “It’s going to still be a while longer before they can actually replace China.”
Modal Motors has two products that it’s developing ahead of Disrupt. One is a small electric motor meant for drones that can also work in fans, blowers, and even actuators. It’s designed to “minimize mass while delivering maximum torque density and efficiency,” according to the startup’s website.
The more radical design is what Modal refers to as the “Hybrid Enigma Drive,” a planar — or flat — electric motor that can fit in lower-profile spaces.
Van Steenburg is drawing on decades of experience in the automotive industry to develop these motors and get them customer-ready. But there’s also an irony in the work Van Steenburg is doing to make Modal Motors’ products a China-free option; in the late 1990s, he worked on a hybrid gas-electric drivetrain that China wanted to put in its so-called “People’s Car.”
“It’s kind of comical,” he said, thinking back on that experience and how much the world has changed. What hasn’t changed, he said, is his outsider streak and strong conviction about doing things that are hard.
“I always tell people that the clock started ticking 25 years ago, and in that whole time, I’ve watched a slow-motion train wreck as China’s been going around the world, grabbing mines, grabbing mineral rights, doing all these things, and slowly but surely monopolizing the entire rare-earth supply chain,” he said.

articles.title: Vicarius launches ScriptAI to write fixes for flaws with no vendor patch - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Vicarius launches ScriptAI to write fixes for flaws with no vendor patch
Vulnerability remediation company Vicarius Inc. today launched an artificial intelligence engine that writes detection and remediation scripts for software flaws with no vendor patch available.
ScriptAI is aimed at the gap between a public disclosure and a working fix. Mean time to exploit stood at negative eight hours as of July on Zero Day Clock data cited this month by Radware Ltd. The same measure gave defenders 53 days in 2024.
Vicarius calls the result a capacity problem rather than a discovery one. Its announcement names Anthropic PBC’s Claude Mythos and Google LLC’s Big Sleep agent as evidence of how quickly machines now surface exploitable code. The fixes still have to be written, the company said.
ScriptAI sits inside the company’s vRx platform. When a vulnerability turns up with no vendor patch behind it, the engine drafts detection and remediation logic, and Vicarius researchers check that logic before anything runs. The platform then executes the script and verifies the result on affected machines. Vicarius said the sequence takes under an hour, against weeks for the same work done by hand.
A deterministic judge issues the pass or fail verdict, the company said, with no language model in the decision path. Each validated case ships with a cryptographically signed evidence manifest. Customers can verify it themselves. Scripts run a pre-check, apply the fix, then verify it and roll back on failure, so a breaking change is caught before it reaches production.
“Finding ten times more vulnerabilities is meaningless if remediation still happens through tickets, manual research and weeks of engineering work,” said Roi Cohen, co-founder and chief executive of Vicarius. “If AI can find the vulnerability, AI should help build the protection.”
Vicarius has done a version of this before. The vuln_GPT model arrived in August 2023, billed as the first trained specifically to write remediation scripts, and its output went out free through the company’s vsociety community. The verification step is what ScriptAI adds.
Everything the engine writes lands in the vScript library under a ScriptAI label. The scripts run as native Bash and PowerShell at the operating system level, with no additional agents or proprietary rule formats.
ScriptAI becomes the fourth path in what Vicarius calls True Remediation. Patching runs through vPatch. When no patch is available, vShield protects the workload, and vScript holds custom and community-sourced remediation scripts.
The new service is available to vRx customers starting today. Vicarius has built remediation tooling out of New York and Tel Aviv since 2016, and Bright Pixel Capital led a $30 million Series B round for the company in January 2024.

articles.title: Travelling to the U.S.? New court ruling allows phone searches without warrant
articles.text:
Canadians travelling to the United States may want to think twice about what’s stored on their phones before crossing the border.
A recent court ruling has affirmed that U.S. border officers can now conduct warrantless searches of travellers’ cellphones without probable cause or even reasonable suspicion.
The decision, issued by the U.S. The Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit on Sept. 17, stemmed from the case of Chinwendu Alisigwe, a permanent U.S. resident whose cellphone was searched by authorities at JFK Airport in New York.
“Under our precedents, no suspicion is required before the government searches a traveller’s property at the border,” read the ruling.
Under U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) policy, officers previously needed reasonable suspicion of a law violation or a national security concern in order to conduct advanced searches.
While this doesn’t necessarily mean that every Canadian who enters the U.S. will have their phone searched, every individual should be aware it could be a possibility for them at the border.
CBP reported that phone searches are relatively uncommon. Latest stats show that of the 419 million international travellers who crossed the border in 2025, officers searched 55,424 devices.
CBP distinguished between basic and advanced searches. A basic search involves an officer looking through the contents of a device, while an advanced search involves connecting external equipment to the device to review and even copy its contents.
Back in 2025, CBP also proposed a new policy that would require Canadians and other travellers to share their social media profiles at the border. However, this proposal was never made official.
For Canadians crossing the border, the main takeaway is to be mindful of what you’re carrying on your phone (laptops and other devices, too) and to delete any sensitive messages, apps, or documents before your trip.
Immigration lawyers and security experts recommend travellers bring a burner phone when visiting the U.S. to keep private information secure. This can help avoid unnecessary scrutiny or data exposure.
The Canadian government warns that officers can search phones, computers, and tablets when Canadians enter the U.S., and they are not required to provide a reason or explanation. Refusing a search could result in your device being seized or being denied entry.
This new ruling comes at a time when relations between Canada and the U.S. have become increasingly strained.
The two countries have been at odds over tariffs and trade, while President Donald Trump has repeatedly made negative comments about Canada and its relationship with the U.S.
Despite these tensions, plenty of Canadians still travel south of the border — however, overall trips have declined significantly.
Statistics Canada reported that return trips from the U.S. fell by 25.4 per cent in 2025, from 39.0 million trips in 2024 to 29.1 million.
The decline was particularly pronounced during the summer, when monthly trips to the U.S. were down by roughly 30 per cent year over year. Florida was one state hit pretty hard by the downturn.
At the same time, more Canadians headed overseas, with international trips rising 9.2 per cent overall.

articles.title: Meta veut que son IA passe vos appels...quitte à les confier à des inconnus
articles.text:
Le 8 septembre dernier, Meta a officiellement déployé aux États-Unis son nouveau modèle baptisé Muse. Il s’agit d’une IA agentique, qui est donc capable d’envoyer des mails, de réserver un voyage et d’effectuer toutes sortes de tâches en ligne. Aussi, Muse devrait être prochainement capable de passer des appels à la place de l’utilisateur. Un rendez-vous à prendre chez le médecin ou une question à poser à une entreprise ? Sur la base de quelques instructions, cette IA peut s’en charger, et elle effectuera ensuite un compte rendu de l’appel à l’utilisateur. Seulement voilà, l’IA pourrait aussi transmettre l’appel à un être humain.
Un appel délégué à une IA qui le transfère ensuite à un centre d’appel
En toute logique, la fonction d’appel de Muse devrait être entièrement gérée par l’intelligence artificielle. L’entreprise américaine a d’ailleurs particulièrement insisté sur le respect de la vie privée de son modèle. Mais selon un rapport de Reuters, qui a pu avoir accès à des documents internes de Meta, Muse pourrait aussi déléguer certains appels à des sous-traitants, autrement dit des humains. Il ne s’agit pas là de rumeurs, mais d’une fonction en cours de test. Dans un document de Meta, il est indiqué que « Muse est désormais en mesure de transmettre les demandes à un agent formé, qui passe l’appel et assure le suivi ».
Un utilisateur de Muse peut donc déléguer un appel à l’IA, qui pourrait à son tour le transférer à un être humain. Bien entendu, le fait que des sous-traitants prennent en charge des appels passés par l’intermédiaire de l’agent IA soulève inévitablement des questions de confidentialité.
Quid de la confidentialité de ces appels ?
Toujours selon Reuters, certains employés de Meta ont averti que des informations sensibles pourraient se retrouver entre les mains des sous-traitants du centre d’appels. S’il est question d’un appel pour prendre rendez-vous chez le coiffeur, cela ne devrait pas poser trop de problèmes. Mais qu’en est-il d’un appel médical ou de toute requête confidentielle auprès d’une entreprise ou d’une administration, pour ne citer que ces exemples ?
Sans surprise, l’entreprise de Mark Zuckerberg s’est montrée confiante quant au fait de déléguer certains appels à des humains. Daniel Roberts, porte-parole de Meta, a déclaré à Reuters que les retours des employés étaient « extrêmement positifs » et que ce test devait permettre à l’entreprise d’affiner les dispositifs de sécurité et de protection de la vie privée avant le lancement de la fonctionnalité. Il a ajouté que Meta ne la déploierait « que lorsqu’il serait prêt et avec les informations appropriées », sans préciser quelles seraient ces informations ni qui les recevrait.
Aussi, nous ne connaissons pas encore les contours de cette fonctionnalité. Un utilisateur pourra-t-il totalement interdire à l’IA de déléguer un appel à un être humain ? Dans tous les cas, cette fonction a assurément une dimension kafkaïenne.

articles.title: Check Point warns of hackers exploiting Security Gateway VPN RCE flaw
articles.text:
Cybersecurity company Check Point has confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-85102, a pre-authentication remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in the VPN certificate-handling functionality of its Security Gateway product.
The same advisory also warns of threat actors exploiting a pre-authentication path traversal flaw tracked as CVE-2026-93616, which impacts the Management web service and can allow script execution and Java class loading.
The company says that CVE-2026-93616 has been exploited as a zero-day since July 23.
On September 10, the Dutch Nationaal Cyber Security Centrum (NCSC) alerted of the Security Gateway issue and urged users to apply available security updates as imminent exploitation was expected.
Check Point has now confirmed that malicious activity started on September 12, with attackers using VPNs and proxies to hide their location.
“Starting September 12, 2026, we observed a wave of exploitation attempts against Spark customers,” reads Check Point’s alert.
“The attempts originated from anonymization infrastructure, including VPN services and proxies," the company said, adding that certificates with the following subjects were used:
- CN=vpn,OU=users,O=global
- CN=vpn-user,OU=users,O=global
- CN=vpnuser,OU=users,O=global
However, the cybersecurity company noted that the three subjects only reflect current observations and more may be in use.
CISA has now added the two flaws in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, urging federal agencies to apply the available fixes and/or mitigations by September 25, 2026.
Mitigating the risk
Check Point’s advisory on CVE-2026-85102 recommends that administrators install Check Point LivePatch Take 26 on supported R81.20, R82, or R82.10 gateways, or install a fixed Jumbo Hotfix: R81.20 Take 166, R82 Take 126, R82.10 Take 44, or R81.10 Take 190, or later.
Customers should also update Spark firewalls to R82.00.10 Build 2325 or R81.10.17 Build 4968, or later.
System administrators are advised to verify if LivePatch is active by running the cpinfo -y CPupdates command on the Security Gateway in expert mode.
The advisory specifically warns that some customers who installed an earlier offline LivePatch package need Take 26 for full coverage.
If updating isn’t possible, it is recommended to disable the VPN implied rules and create explicit rules that restrict Site-to-Site VPN on UDP/500 and UDP/4500 to specific peer IP addresses.
For Remote Access VPN, allow only the required services over UDP/500, UDP/4500, TCP/443, and TCP/80 where applicable, and restrict source client IP ranges where possible.
Check Point notes that these mitigation measures do not apply to locally managed Spark firewalls.
For mitigation and hunting advice for the Management web service CVE-2026-93616, Check Point points to this support article.

articles.title: Attention, Muse, l'IA de Meta, peut être piratée par une simple commande sur votre Mac
articles.text:
Le chercheur en sécurité Patrick Wardle a découvert une faille zero-day dans Muse, l'assistant IA de Meta pour Mac. Une simple commande locale suffit à détourner l'agent pour intercepter la voix de l'utilisateur et prendre le contrôle de ses comptes connectés.
Muse, l'IA que Meta vient de lancer, n'est pas passée inaperçue et connait un succès fulgurant auprès du public et des investisseurs… mais aussi un blocage par Amazon pour des raisons de sécurité. Ars Technica détaille faille technique qui alimente ces inquiétudes.
Comment une commande de terminal peut voler la voix et le compte
Muse dicte les messages vocaux via un serveur de Meta, lequel se charge de les transcrire. Patrick Wardle, fondateur de la fondation Objective-See et spécialiste de la sécurité macOS, a découvert qu'une appli locale ou une simple commande de terminal peut changer l'adresse de ce serveur, sans demander la moindre autorisation sur macOS. Il suffit alors de rediriger ce trafic vers un serveur piégé pour récupérer à la fois les échanges vocaux et le jeton qui authentifie le compte Muse de la victime.
Avec ce jeton, l'attaquant hérite de toutes les autorisations accordées à Muse. Cela inclut lire les e-mails, gérer l'agenda, se connecter à WhatsApp ou aux réseaux sociaux, et parfois accéder aux fichiers, au micro, à la caméra ou à la localisation via les permissions macOS. Apple encadre normalement ce type d'accès pour bloquer les applications et commandes de terminal indésirables. Muse contourne cette protection en s'appuyant sur les autorisations déjà accordées par l'utilisateur.
Pour en arriver là, l'attaquant doit d'abord réussir à exécuter du code sur le Mac, via un malware, une application piégée ou de l'ingénierie sociale. Mais il n'a pas besoin de compromettre toute la machine. Une seule commande, obtenue par une technique de type ClickFix suffit. Wardle a réalisé plusieurs démonstrations de ce détournement avec l'écriture de fichiers sur le disque, la prise de photo à distance, le tout, sans le moindre signal visible pour l'utilisateur.
Alors si vous souhaitiez installer Muse… mieux vaut sans doute y réfléchir à deux fois. Plus généralement, mieux vaut limiter les connexions données d'emblée à un agent IA (messagerie, agenda, paiement, permissions système), les revoir régulièrement, et se méfier de toute demande d'autorisation inhabituelle. Reste à savoir si Meta corrigera ce problème. Garder son système à jour, utiliser un antivirus actif et ignorer les commandes trouvées sur un site ou dans un message non sollicité restent les bons réflexes face à ce genre de faille.

articles.title: Amazon blocked Meta's Muse. Then Shopify wired it into every store.
articles.text:
Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse. Then Shopify wired it into every store.
Amazon started blocking Meta’s Muse from browsing and buying on Amazon.com on Sunday, roughly two weeks after the personal agent launched on September 8. Shoppers who ask Muse to buy something there now get a pop-up telling them that continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use.
Amazon’s objections have little to do with shopping itself. Meta never told Amazon that Muse would visit the store, the agent does not identify itself while it browses, and it appears to capture and store customer credentials. Those three properties describe almost every personal agent shipping this year. Grok Bot from xAI also drives signed-in browser sessions, and so does the open-source OpenClaw project that Muse is modeled on. The block is a category design problem rather than a disagreement between two companies.
What Amazon actually blocked
Muse runs on a dedicated virtual machine that Meta calls Muse Secure VM, and it reaches services in two ways: It uses built-in connectors for partners such as Gmail and OpenTable, and it drives an ordinary browser session for everything else. Shopping on Amazon.com used the second path.
That second path is what Amazon objects to. From the server’s side, a browser-driving agent looks like a signed-in customer with unusually fast reflexes, moving through search, product pages, account history, and checkout without ever declaring what it is. Amazon told GeekWire it asked Meta to exclude the store voluntarily, but Meta did not agree before the block went live.
The credential dispute is harder to settle from outside. Meta says Muse has no visibility into passwords or payment methods and that credentials sit in secure storage, while Amazon says the agent appears to capture and retain them. Both statements may be sincere, and the merchant can verify neither, since an unannounced session provides no evidence of which software holds the password.
The legal ground shifted seven weeks ago
Amazon reached for its Conditions of Use rather than the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Those terms, updated August 14, now require agents to identify themselves in user-agent strings and stop when asked. The likely reason sits in a ruling from early August. The Ninth Circuit vacated the preliminary injunction Amazon had won against Perplexity, and the panel held that a user directing the Comet assistant is the party accessing Amazon’s computers. Writing for the court, Judge Milan Smith described the assistant as a tool, not a person, for statutory purposes.
If you’re operating a public API or storefront, the ruling makes lawsuits a weaker tool for keeping agents out. Blocking them in your own infrastructure is now the more reliable option. A site cannot easily argue that an agent trespassed, so it has to decide for itself which automated clients it admits, publish that decision, and enforce it in its own infrastructure. Amazon’s pop-up is that enforcement, written in product rather than in a filing.
The identity layer already exists
Platform teams have solved a version of this problem before. Inside a service mesh, no workload is trusted by default because it looks like a normal client, and every call carries a verifiable identity that the receiving service checks before applying policy. Agent traffic on the public web faces the same requirement, and the specification is further along than most teams realize.
An IETF draft called Web Bot Auth builds on HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421). An agent signs its requests with a private key and publishes the matching public key at a well-known directory on its own domain. The verifier reads the Signature-Agent header, fetches the key set, and learns which operator is calling. Cloudflare validates these signatures at its edge for verified bots and agents. AWS WAF Bot Control added the same support for CloudFront distributions in November 2025.
The limits matter as much as the mechanism. A signature identifies the operator behind the agent, not the person it is acting for. The merchant learns that a request came from a named vendor, without learning whose account is in use or what the shopper approved. Amazon’s complaint about stored credentials sits in that gap. Signed identity settles the disclosure question and leaves authorization open.
Shopify took the other route within a day
While Amazon was blocking Muse, Shopify was wiring it in. On September 21, the two companies announced agentic checkout with Shop Pay across Shopify stores, extending the arrangement that made Meta an AI channel in Shopify Catalog on the day Muse launched. Muse reads structured product data and completes payment through a declared path, so the merchant knows an agent is transacting, and each purchase draws a single-use credential, so the card number never reaches Muse.
The plumbing for that path is public. Google and Shopify’s Universal Commerce Protocol covers discovery, cart, and checkout. The Agentic Commerce Protocol from OpenAI and Stripe covers checkout execution while the merchant stays the system of record. Google’s Agent Payments Protocol, donated to the FIDO Alliance in April, includes proof of the shopper’s authorization. A merchant that adopts it gets identity, scope, and an audit trail in the same transaction, which is what Amazon says it wanted and did not get.
Both routes follow from the business underneath them. Amazon runs its own storefront, recommendations, and assistant, so an outside agent that hides its identity takes the customer relationship and gives nothing measurable in return. Shopify sells infrastructure to merchants, so every new agent channel that reads its catalog and settles through Shop Pay reinforces the rails underneath. The key difference is who owns the demand surface, which explains why the same agent got a block from one company and a partnership from the other in the same 24 hours.
Choosing how to handle agent traffic
Most teams exposing an API or a storefront now have to make this call deliberately rather than by default. The decision depends on how much the business relies on the customer relationship at the point of contact and whether an agent can be identified when the customer arrives.
| Scenario | Recommended option | Rationale | 
|---|---|---|
| Public content and catalog data, no account access | Verify signatures at the edge and allow named agents | Web Bot Auth is checked by default on Cloudflare and AWS WAF, so the cost is policy configuration rather than engineering, though it tells you the operator and not the shopper | 
| Agent transactions where you want the revenue | Publish a declared channel using ACP, UCP, or an MCP server | Structured access gives scope and an audit trail, at the cost of building and maintaining a second interface alongside the site | 
| Account access with stored credentials | Require a scoped token, never a replayed password | Delegated tokens can be revoked per agent, though few consumer agents support them yet, which pushes the burden back onto your login flow | 
| Competitive surfaces you intend to keep | State the rule in terms of service and enforce it at the edge | Legally durable after the Ninth Circuit ruling, though it invites the same public standoff Amazon is now in | 
Most real deployments will combine these rows rather than pick one. A retailer can verify signed agents on product pages, route purchases through a declared checkout, and still refuse an unannounced browser session inside a logged-in account. That combination is closer to Amazon’s position than its pop-up suggests.
What platform teams should do this quarter
Enterprise buyers and the teams running these systems face the same three questions, in a specific order.
Decide what an unidentified agent may do
The first question to settle is admission, and most sites have not settled it. They treat agent traffic as either a scraper to block or a browser to serve, and neither answer survives contact with a customer who wants an agent to act for them. Write policies for public pages, logged-in pages, and checkout separately, then publish them where an agent vendor can find them.
Give identified agents somewhere better to go
The second question is substitution, and it decides whether the first one holds. Blocking a browser-driving agent without offering a structured path leaves the demand intact and pushes it toward workarounds. Sabre reported that nearly 80 of its customers now pilot or run its MCP server for booking rather than let agents work through a booking screen. A catalog feed, an MCP server, or an ACP endpoint converts hostile traffic into a channel you can meter.
Fix credential handling before agents force it
The third question is authorization, and Amazon raised it loudest. An agent replaying a stored password is indistinguishable from credential stuffing at the network layer, regardless of any goodwill between the two companies. Scoped, revocable tokens tied to a named agent and a spending limit are the only version a risk owner can approve.
Where agent access is headed
Amazon and Meta will settle this commercially, because Amazon has an advertising arrangement that lets Facebook and Instagram users shop its products, and Meta buys compute from AWS, and neither gains from a long standoff over one shopping flow. The precedent is already set regardless of how they settle. Every site that matters to an agent now has to answer whether it admits anonymous automation, and it will enforce that answer through bot management rules and protocol endpoints rather than cease-and-desist letters.
Agent builders should read the block as an argument for declaring themselves. An agent that signs its requests, identifies its operator, and transacts via a published protocol can be allowed, rate-limited, and billed, while one that arrives disguised as a browser will keep encountering pop-ups. For developers building the services these agents reach, the signed identity layer arriving through Cloudflare, AWS, and the commerce protocols is the most useful infrastructure the open web has gained in years. It is worth adopting before the next agent shows up unannounced.

articles.title: Google, Apple y Microsoft han coincidido en la misma semana en algo que nadie esperaba: el ordenador vuelve a importar
articles.text:
En apenas dos días han pasado tres grandes noticias para el ordenador como concepto:
- Google ha puesto nombre, precio, especificaciones y fecha a los primeros Googlebook, portátiles con Android y Gemini integrado.
- Han llegado los primeros análisis del Mac mini M6 y el Mac Studio M5 Ultra. Varias coinciden en que son máquinas estupendas para ejecutar agentes de IA en local.
- Microsoft ha explicado en detalle a The Pragmatic Engineer cómo tratará Windows a esos agentes cuya integración anunció hace unos meses: como usuarios con identidad propia.
Tras quince años viendo cómo el móvil ha ido acaparando el protagonismo, con el ordenador relegado a dispositivo secundario con las excepciones de transiciones de arquitectura (Apple Silicon y también ARM en Windows), ahora las tres grandes apuestan a la vez por lo contrario. El motivo es el mismo en los tres casos: los agentes necesitan algo que el móvil no puede darles.
Por qué con el móvil no basta
El smartphone se ha construido sobre la idea de que cada aplicación vive en su sandbox y no puede tocar la de al lado. Eso es lo que lo hizo seguro y distintos a los ordenadores. También es lo que lo vuelve hostil para un agente, cuyo trabajo consiste justo en saltar de una caja a otra: leer un correo, consultar el calendario, hacer una reserva, guardar un PDF...
Muse, el agente de Meta, es un gran ejemplo reciente: asigna a cada usuario un ordenador virtual en la nube que navega, completa tareas y sigue trabajando aunque se cierre la app. Se usa desde el móvil, pero no trabaja en él. El móvil es un mando a distancia porque el trabajo real ocurre en un ordenador de Meta. Lo mismo aplica a Instinct o a Grok Bot.
La bolsa también lo ha leído así. El lunes, ARM subió un 17%, Intel un 12% y AMD un 10%, en un rally atribuido a la buena acogida de Muse: mantener encendidos esos ordenadores virtuales requiere procesadores, pero no tarjetas gráficas. Ninguno de los tres fabricantes había anunciado nada, por cierto.
Tres empresas y una misma apuesta
En la próxima versión de Windows, un agente con identidad local aparecerá en el Administrador de Tareas como un usuario más. Tiene sentido: sus sesiones duran horas y usa varios programas a la vez, exactamente igual que un humano. Un sistema operativo pensado para alguien sentado ante el teclado se va a adaptar a un usuario que no tiene manos pero que cada vez importa más.
Google, por su parte, renuncia a su tesis anterior. El Chromebook que hemos visto durante casi tres lustros partía de que el portátil no importaba demasiado, así que lo enfocaron como una ventana barata al navegador. El Googlebook en cambio juega en la liga del MacBook, y Rick Osterloh lo ha descrito en The Verge como el gran movimiento de enfoque de la empresa. Google ya no quiere que el ordenador sea irrelevante. Quiere que sea, ante todo, suyo.
En el caso de Apple, lo notable del Mac Studio no es su rendimiento, que ya conocíamos y dábamos por descontado, sino lo bien que le viene el salto a ARM y memoria unificada que hicieron en 2020. Una arquitectura que lo hace especialmente idóneo para usar IA en local, incluidos agentes.
El ordenador sirve a los agentes porque es abierto: cualquier programa puede leer ficheros o tocar la configuración de otro. Es justo lo que el móvil cerró, y es justo la costura que ya mostrado Muse a su pesar: Ars Technica ha encontrado un fallo en su versión para Mac: cualquier aplicación podía redirigir el dictado a un servidor del atacante y quedarse con el token de la cuenta. Meta solo tardó unas horas en parchearlo, pero la lección no se olvida: un agente con acceso a correo, pagos y disco multiplica el daño de cualquier malware. No es casual que Amazon citara la seguridad al bloquear a Muse.
La respuesta de Microsoft, la de dar una identidad a cada agente, recupera una idea tan antigua como las cuentas de usuario para separar lo que cada uno puede tocar y lo que no. La diferencia es que ahora muchos de esos usuarios no son personas.
El ordenador importa más justo cuando es más caro tenerlo
Mientras tanto, el mercado del PC se está hundiendo. IDC prevé una caída de ventas superior al 11% este año, en parte por la escasez de RAM y NAND que provocan los centros de datos de IA. Ya hemos visto cómo esto está alterando la venta de ordenadores y ya nadie puede escapar al subidón de precios por las memorias.
Conviven así dos modelos:
- En uno, el agente vive en tu ordenador.
- En el otro, tu ordenador vive en el centro de datos de otro.
La subida en bolsa del lunes fue una apuesta por el segundo modelo, y la crisis de la RAM empuja en esa dirección: si la RAM se va a los centros de datos, el ordenador capaz de alojar un agente también acaba allí.
Durante años nos hemos preguntado si en algún momento el móvil remataría al ordenador mediante una convergencia que llevamos mucho tiempo esperando sin que haya avanzado gran cosa. La respuesta ha sido otra: vuelve a ser imprescindible porque quien lo usa ya no es solo quien se sienta delante. La pregunta para los próximos años no va a ser únicamente "qué ordenador compro" sino "en el ordenador de quién vive el agente que actúa por mí".
El ordenador ha vuelto. Lo que no está claro es que vuelva a ser nuestro.

articles.title: XPENG L03 : le SUV coupé qui mise sur l'intelligence artificielle embarquée
articles.text:
XPENG L03 : le SUV coupé qui mise sur l'intelligence artificielle embarquée
Sous le capot du nouveau XPENG L03, ce n'est plus un moteur qu'on regarde en premier, mais une puce. Trois, en réalité pour la version Ultra. Le SUV coupé chinois embarque un supercalculateur maison censé redéfinir ce qu'on attend d'une voiture pilotée par l'intelligence artificielle. Décryptage d'une architecture qui sort des standards habituels du secteur.
Le chiffre interpelle forcément : 2 250 TOPS. C'est la puissance de calcul cumulée des trois puces Turing conçues par XPENG, chacune développant 750 TOPS. À titre de comparaison, la majorité des véhicules dits "intelligents" sur le marché plafonnent aujourd'hui sous les 200 TOPS. L'écart est donc conséquent, presque d'un autre ordre de grandeur.
XPENG a fait le choix de ne pas s'appuyer sur des fournisseurs tiers pour cette brique technologique, contrairement à une large partie de l'industrie. Une décision qui s'inscrit dans une logique d'intégration verticale, où le constructeur maîtrise à la fois le matériel et les algorithmes qui tournent dessus. Tout maîtriser de A à Z, à court terme, ça coûte moins cher et cela se répercute évidemment sur le prix de ventes des voitures.
Trois puces pour trois missions
Le principe retenu se veut simple sur le papier : plutôt que de faire porter toutes les tâches à un seul processeur, XPENG répartit le travail. Deux puces sont réservées à la conduite autonome et à la sécurité active, pilotées par le système VLA 2.0 associé au VLMU. La troisième s'occupe exclusivement du cockpit intelligent XOS 6, capable de faire tourner localement un modèle d'intelligence artificielle de 30 milliards de paramètres, soit un assistant embarqué qui n'a pas systématiquement besoin d'une connexion pour répondre.
Cette séparation des tâches a une utilité assez concrète pour le client, car elle évite qu'une fonction de confort ne vienne ralentir un calcul lié à la sécurité, et inversement. Sur le terrain, cela se traduit par 17 fonctions de sécurité active proposées de série, un chiffre supérieur à ce que propose généralement la concurrence sur ce segment.
Des automatismes pensés pour le quotidien
Au-delà des chiffres, deux fonctions retiennent l'attention parce qu'elles répondent à des situations très concrètes. Le « Custom Parking » permet de mémoriser une manœuvre de stationnement récurrente, utile pour qui gare sa voiture tous les soirs dans le même parking résidentiel un peu tarabiscoté. Le « Trace Reverse » de son côté, assiste la marche arrière autonome dans une impasse, en repassant par le chemin emprunté à l'aller.
Le L03 s'appuie par ailleurs sur une transmission intégrale AWD pour la version Ultra, une autonomie WLTP annoncée dans la moyenne haute du segment, et une recharge ultra-rapide censée limiter les arrêts sur autoroute. Le tout est appelé à évoluer dans le temps grâce à des mises à jour OTA régulières. Une manière, pour XPENG, de vendre non pas seulement une voiture figée mais une base technique amenée à progresser après l'achat.
Reste la question de la confiance, centrale pour un acheteur professionnel ou CSP+ qui n'a pas forcément grandi avec la marque : XPENG accompagne le L03 d'une garantie constructeur de 7 ans et d'une assistance routière, deux éléments qui pèsent souvent autant dans la décision que la fiche technique elle-même.

articles.title: NVIDIA Smooth Motion Reaches GeForce RTX 30-Series "Ampere" GPUs Through Mods
articles.text:
Wednesday, September 23rd 2026
	
									
	
	
	
NVIDIA Smooth Motion Reaches GeForce RTX 30-Series "Ampere" GPUs Through Mods
Modders have gotten NVIDIA's Smooth Motion frame generation running on GeForce RTX 30 series cards, VideoCardz reports. Smooth Motion is NVIDIA's driver-level frame generation feature, similar in spirit to AMD's AFMF, and NVIDIA only exposes it officially on RTX 40-series and newer through the NVIDIA App. Ampere owners have been left out, at least officially. Two unrelated projects are apparently working to close that gap. 
The first comes from developer pipotoufikxyz-lgtm, who expanded the earlier dlssg_for_sm86 project, itself an adaptation of NVIDIA's DLSS-G runtime for the SM86 architecture that RTX 30 GPUs use. The update adds Smooth Motion and Vulkan support, and it reportedly went live on September 19, tested on an RTX 3070. The second, NVSmooth30, comes from a developer going by ItsAdeline and takes a different route: rather than building on the existing DLSS-G package, it's a clean-room compatibility layer aimed directly at NVIDIA's NvPresent64.dll Smooth Motion path. Currently, NVSmooth30 has been tested on an RTX 3050 laptop GPU, and separately on an RTX 3070.While a great technical achievement, neither mod looks plug-and-play at this time. It's also relevant to remind readers this isn't the same thing as Frame Generation or Multi-Frame Generation, both of which are designed to take advantage of hardware present in RTX 40- and 50-series, respectively. There's also the usual caveat with anything touching game files: it can trip anti-cheat systems, so competitive online games are probably worth avoiding. Nonetheless, two teams independently landing on working implementations does seemingly suggest Smooth Motion isn't hardware-locked out of Ampere, at least not technically. Whether NVIDIA ever turns that into official support for RTX 30-series owners is a different matter, and nothing points to that happening any time soon.

articles.title: Raspberry Pi's RAM lock was built to stop scalpers, but it's blocking repairs too
articles.text:
Winners & losers: Raspberry Pi has confirmed that its firmware prevents users from changing a board's factory RAM configuration, a restriction that blocks not only unofficial memory upgrades but also some attempts to replace failed RAM chips with equivalent parts. The company says the measure is meant to stop resellers from passing off untested, modified boards as factory configurations, but it also limits a capability long used by Raspberry Pi repair and maker communities.
The issue came up on the Raspberry Pi forums after a user replaced the RAM on a Compute Module 5 but couldn't get the board to recognize the new 4 GB chip. PhilE, a Raspberry Pi engineer and forum moderator, said the company has been "locking devices to their original RAM size" for some time.
The firmware does more than check capacity. It also stores other attributes linked to the original memory device, according to PhilE. That could prevent even a same-capacity replacement chip from working. For users trying to fix a failed RAM IC, the limit could make a board impossible to repair even when a compatible replacement part is available.
Raspberry Pi said the policy is meant to stop untested modified boards from entering the resale market. The company said some resellers could buy lower-memory products, install larger chips "of dubious origin," and sell them as factory 8 GB models.
"If labor is cheap enough then there may be a minor financial gain in buying a part with say a 2GB part, swapping it for an 8GB part of dubious origin, and reselling it as an 8GB device," PhilE wrote.
Those modified boards may have stability problems because Raspberry Pi did not test them in their altered configuration. Buyers could still contact Raspberry Pi for support, however, leaving the company responsible for problems caused by third-party modifications. Raspberry Pi's answer is to eliminate the upgrade option in the first place.
PhilE was direct about the result for users attempting a RAM swap: "don't waste your time trying - it won't work."
The restriction also applies to users who are not trying to create unofficial higher-spec models. Raspberry Pi boards have long been used in home labs, embedded products, edge deployments and custom hardware. A developer may find that an existing board no longer has enough memory for a new workload, while a repair technician may want to replace a failed chip without changing the device's specification. Under the firmware policy, neither use case is guaranteed to work.
The lock reportedly began rolling out in firmware updates in late 2024. It was therefore in place before the recent increase in RAM prices tied to demand from AI data centers. Raspberry Pi's explanation points instead to product validation, resale practices and support costs.
Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 5 users have demonstrated memory upgrades by removing and replacing BGA-mounted RAM packages. Such work requires specialized soldering equipment and carries obvious risks, but it showed that the hardware could support higher-capacity configurations.
Because of the current firmware, a user might still be able to complete the physical work, but the board could reject the altered memory configuration. Users may need to revert to an older firmware version to bypass the restriction, if one is available for that model.
The policy may frustrate Raspberry Pi's repair and maker communities, which have long treated the company's hardware as unusually open for low-cost computing platforms. Some supporters have suggested a warranty flag or one-time setting that would identify a modified board and remove Raspberry Pi support without blocking the modification itself.
Raspberry Pi has instead chosen to enforce the original RAM configuration in firmware. For most users, the change will have little effect. For repair shops, developers and hardware modders, it removes one more option.

articles.title: Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu says global tech cos cannot ask entire industry to slow down on AI
articles.text:
Zoho’s Sridhar Vembu says global tech cos cannot ask entire industry to slow down on AI
LLMs are becoming a commodity, with too many models in the market and prices also falling, Vembu said on the sidelines of the Zoholics event in Chennai.
Sridhar Vembu, Chief Scientist and Co-founder of global tech company Zoho, said he views calls by global technology companies for a slowdown in AI development with cynicism.
"These companies have the freedom to slow down... If I want to slow down, I can... but I cannot ask the entire industry to slow down... I see this a little more cynically," said Vembu, adding that global AI companies want everybody else to go slow so they can move faster and monopolise the market.
Large language models (LLMs) are becoming a commodity, with too many models in the market and prices also crashing, Vembu said on the sidelines of the Zoholics user conference in Chennai. In the current industry landscape, companies cannot meet profit objectives or justify their valuation on the evolving token economics, he said, adding that's why they are probably calling for a slowdown.
Global AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic have recently called for the industry to slow the pace of frontier AI development, amid escalating security concerns. At the same time, both Anthropic and OpenAI have launched their latest AI models, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol respectively.
AI in coding
Commenting on the widespread use of AI in coding, Vembu said while code is generated by AI, organisations cannot hide behind it to avoid accountability. "We cannot tell customers that the system broke (if something goes wrong). We are ultimately responsible for the software... I tell software engineers to use AI but not become so dependent on it that they don't even understand what they are doing."
He had recently tweeted about this as well. "I tell our engineers to use AI but never cede our understanding to AI... As an industry, we are driving too fast in a fancy new car we barely understand how to drive, inviting disaster," he posted on X.

articles.title: Usan paneles solares y baterías de litio en Festival Cordillera en Colombia: sin diésel durante dos días
articles.text:
El Festival Cordillera 2026 marcó un precedente en la industria de eventos masivos en Colombia al operar una de sus áreas de servicio con energía prácticamente libre de combustibles fósiles. La zona de baños VIP número 2 funcionó durante las dos jornadas del festival con un sistema híbrido de generación solar y almacenamiento en baterías, desarrollado por Caban Energy, Klik y Páramo Impacta, que alcanzó un consumo 96,58 % limpio y renovable.
La instalación, compuesta por 24 paneles solares y seis baterías de litio, se convirtió así en la primera de su tipo dentro de un festival colombiano y sirvió como prueba de campo para evaluar el desempeño de estas tecnologías en condiciones reales de alta demanda.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo funcionó el sistema de energía solar y baterías en el festival
El esquema instalado en Cordillera 2026 combinó generación fotovoltaica con almacenamiento en baterías de litio con tecnología LFP. Durante el día, los 24 paneles solares, de 620 Wp cada uno, captaron la radiación solar y suministraron energía de forma directa a la zona de baños.
Una parte de esa energía se destinó al funcionamiento inmediato del servicio, mientras que el excedente se almacenó en seis baterías de litio. Este mecanismo permitió que, una vez caída la noche y sin luz solar disponible, el sistema siguiera entregando energía limpia sin interrupciones.
El monitoreo y control de toda la operación estuvo a cargo de Continuo, la plataforma tecnológica de Caban Energy, encargada de supervisar el comportamiento del sistema durante los dos días de festival.
PUBLICIDAD
En términos de capacidad, la instalación contó con una potencia solar de 14,8 kWp y una capacidad de almacenamiento de 28,8 kWh. Un sistema de energía solar con baterías es una solución que capta la radiación del sol durante el día para uso inmediato y almacena el excedente en baterías de litio, de modo que pueda utilizarse por la noche o cuando no hay generación solar, sin depender de combustibles fósiles.
Resultados de generación y ahorro energético logrado
Durante las dos jornadas del Festival Cordillera 2026, el sistema generó 44 kWh de energía a partir de fuentes solares. De ese total, se registró una carga de batería de 32,6 kWh y una descarga de 20,7 kWh, cifras que reflejan cómo operó el ciclo de almacenamiento y suministro a lo largo del evento.
PUBLICIDAD
Más allá de los datos de generación, la implementación tuvo un efecto directo sobre el uso de combustibles tradicionales. El sistema permitió ahorrar alrededor de 1,3 litros de diésel por hora, lo que se tradujo en un ahorro total de 5 galones durante los dos días de operación.
Esa reducción, según se explica, equivale aproximadamente a las emisiones que generaría un automóvil de combustión al recorrer 127 kilómetros. El dato ilustra el impacto ambiental de reemplazar, incluso de forma parcial, la generación con diésel por fuentes renovables en un evento de alta demanda energética.
Por qué esta prueba energética cobra relevancia en el contexto climático actual
La implementación de esta microrred no ocurre de manera aislada. Se enmarca en un contexto climático descrito por expertos como uno de los fenómenos de El Niño más intensos desde 1950.
PUBLICIDAD
Investigadores han señalado riesgos asociados a sequías, calor extremo, menor nivel de embalses, incendios y afectaciones marinas para el período comprendido entre octubre y diciembre. Este panorama incrementa la necesidad de diversificar las fuentes de generación energética disponibles en el país.
En ese sentido, la combinación de energía solar y almacenamiento en baterías se presenta como una alternativa que permite gestionar la energía de manera más flexible, aprovechando las horas de mayor radiación solar para disponer de esa energía posteriormente, bajo demanda, incluso cuando la generación fotovoltaica directa no está disponible.
Qué representa esta experiencia para la industria de festivales en Colombia
La prueba realizada en Cordillera 2026 funcionó como un banco de pruebas real para tecnologías que buscan reducir la dependencia de fuentes fósiles en eventos masivos, donde la continuidad del servicio eléctrico resulta indispensable para la operación durante toda su duración.
PUBLICIDAD
El hecho de que la zona de baños VIP haya operado con 96,58 % de energía limpia y renovable demuestra que es posible incorporar fuentes de generación solar y sistemas de almacenamiento en infraestructuras temporales de alta exigencia, sin comprometer la continuidad del servicio.
Esta experiencia se suma a un conjunto de iniciativas que exploran cómo la industria del entretenimiento puede avanzar hacia esquemas de generación con menor dependencia de combustibles fósiles, en un momento en que las condiciones climáticas exigen mayor flexibilidad y diversificación en las fuentes de energía disponibles.
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Sony INZONE M10S II 27-inch 540 Hz QHD OLED gaming monitor review: A major player in a crowded field
articles.text:
Tom's Hardware Verdict
Sony’s INZONE M10SII is a superb gaming monitor for competitive or casual play. It delivers a sharp, textural, and colorful image and a premium gaming experience.
Pros
- +Sharp, textural and colorful image
- +Matte screen rejects ambient light better than competitors
- +Flexible refresh modes up to 720 Hz
- +Smooth and response gaming feel
- +Premium build quality
Cons
- -No LED lighting or internal speakers
Why you can trust Tom's Hardware
When I look at my collection of computer monitor reviews from the past 13 years, I see a tremendous number of displays from manufacturers that begin with the letter A. But there are lesser-represented companies with the same level of engineering expertise and high quality as mainstream brands when it comes to the best gaming monitors.
If you’re old enough to remember CRTs, then you’ve heard of the Sony Trinitron tube. This was an evolved display with a cylindrical shape rather than the bubble screens that fronted other CRTs. It wasn’t completely flat, but it curved only along one axis. And it was coveted by users for its sharp and undistorted image.
Today, you can still buy a premium gaming monitor from Sony, and here is its latest: the INZONE M10S II. It’s a 27-inch OLED with QHD resolution and 540 Hz refresh rate. It runs at 720 Hz in HD and supports Adaptive-Sync, HDR, and wide-gamut color. Let’s take a look.
Sony INZONE M10S II Specs
| Panel Type / Backlight | Organic Light Emitting Diode (OLED) | 
| Screen Size / Aspect Ratio | 27 inches / 16:9 | 
| Max Resolution and Refresh Rate | 2560x1440 @ 540 Hz | 
| Row 3 - Cell 0 | 1280x720 @ 720 Hz | 
| Row 4 - Cell 0 | FreeSync and G-Sync Compatible | 
| Native Color Depth and Gamut | 10-bit / DCI-P3+ | 
| Response Time (GTG) | 0.02ms | 
| Brightness | 283 nits full field | 
| Row 8 - Cell 0 | 543 nits 25% window | 
| Contrast | Unmeasurable | 
| Speakers | None | 
| Video Inputs | 1x DisplayPort 2.1 | 
| Row 12 - Cell 0 | 2x HDMI 2.1 | 
| Audio | 3.5mm headphone output | 
| USB 3.2 | 1x up, 2x down | 
| Power Consumption | 43.5w, brightness @ 200 nits | 
| Panel Dimensions WxHxD w/base | 23.8 x 14.9-19.7 x 7.8 inches (604 x 378-500 x 197mm) | 
| Panel Thickness | 2.28 inches (58mm) | 
| Bezel Width | Top: 0.28 inch (7mm) | 
| Row 19 - Cell 0 | Top/sides: 0.3 inch (8mm) | 
| Row 20 - Cell 0 | Bottom: 0.47 inch (12mm) | 
| Weight | 13.64 pounds (6.2kg) | 
| Warranty | 3 years | 
The M10S II starts with an OLED panel that runs natively at 2560x1440 QHD resolution and 540 Hz. A dual-refresh mode bumps that up to 720 Hz at HD, 1280x720 pixels. Adaptive-Sync runs on both AMD and Nvidia platforms, and you get HDR support with the ability to calibrate for HDR10 content. The screen coating is unusual in that it’s matte, while nearly every OLED that crosses my desk is shiny. That finish is extremely effective at rejecting image-spoiling ambient light. It literally swallows up reflections and displays the image without any visible grain.
The M10S II delivers a huge color gamut that, in my tests, covered nearly 110% of DCI-P3. I found that calibration was necessary, but the reward was a beautifully saturated image. There’s an sRGB mode available if you need that smaller gamut for photography or graphics work. You also get variable brightness to stretch dynamic range. It has two settings that had a positive impact in both practice and testing. I’ll tell you more about that on page four. Peak output is around 475 nits in SDR mode and 543 nits in HDR mode when measuring a 25% window pattern.
For gaming, you get plenty of goodness in the form of static and dynamic aiming points, OLED anti-flicker, black frame insertion for blur reduction at low frame rates, an FPS indicator, and a set of timers. Missing are internal speakers and LED lighting, but you do get USB ports for peripherals. There’s panel protection in the form of advanced heat management and OLED care options, such as panel refresh and pixel orbiting. The latest I/O ports also include one DisplayPort 2.1 and two HDMI 2.1 ports. A pair of headphones can be plugged into the provided 3.5mm jack. There’s a comprehensive OSD for control, or you can use Sony’s INZONE Hub app, which is free to download.
The M10S II sells for $1,100 at this writing, so it’s primed to compete with other speedy competition displays. While it isn’t quite as loaded as an Asus ROG Swift screen, it delivers equal performance and image quality.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Assembly and Accessories
The M10S II’s carton gets the full cardboard treatment with no crumbly foam in sight. The panel, upright, and base assemble without tools. If you plan to use an arm, there’s a 100mm VESA mount with fasteners included. Also in the box are a DisplayPort cable, an external power brick, and a sheet of INZONE stickers, in case you want to decorate your Trapper Keeper.
Product 360
The M10S II’s most visible feature is its small-footprint base. Honestly, when I took it out of the box, I was dubious about its stability. It’s a heavy metal disc just six inches across. The upright bolts to its center with an offset that extends the depth to almost eight inches. It looks like it would fall over easily, but I gave it a few shakes, and it remained stable. This is geometry at work. The swivel point is where the upright and base meet, allowing you to swing the screen 360 degrees. You also get a 5/35-degree tilt and a 4.8-inch height range, no portrait mode, though. Movements are firm and smooth with no wobble or play.
Reach around the back right, and you’ll find a small protrusion with a power button and a joystick for the OSD. Uniquely, the power LED is positioned on the side, just the right spot to light up your hand when you press the button. It isn’t visible from the front, but you can turn it off if you wish.
The side view shows a thick component bulge attached to a thin screen backed by a metal plate. It’s just 5mm thick, and the bezel is narrow too: 7mm on top, 8mm on the sides, and 12mm at the bottom. It’s flush, so you can’t see it when the power’s off.
The I/O panel is up and under and includes two HDMI 2.1 ports, one DisplayPort 2.1, and USB, one upstream and two downstream ports. There are no internal speakers, so you can plug headphones into the 3.5mm jack. An additional USB port is there for service and firmware updates.
OSD Features
Pressing the M10S II’s joystick brings up an efficiently organized OSD. It’s divided into nine sections and has plenty of calibration and convenience options.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The OSD begins with picture modes, eight in total. The default is Game, and it looks good but needs a bit of tweaking to align it with broadcast standards. The other modes are aimed at specific game types or tasks, and there’s an accurate sRGB mode. I found the best results using Standard with a grayscale calibration, which you can read about below and on page four.
Gaming Assist includes the refresh rate switches and 24.5-inch modes which deliver 1080 vertical pixels while maintaining a 1:1 mapping. That way, there’s no scaling to soften the image. You also get motion blur reduction via a backlight strobe, which works well at low frame rates. It cuts brightness by around 30%. Anti-VRR flicker is unique to OLED monitors and prevents flickering during rapid frame-rate transitions. Hint: if your video card is fast enough to keep the action above 300 Hz, you won’t get flicker. Also in this menu are an FPS counter and aiming points, both static and dynamic.
In the Picture adjustment menu, you’ll find the variable brightness options, which Sony calls Brightness stabilizer. It’s counter to other monitors I’ve encountered, in that off means variable brightness is fully engaged. I experimented with all three settings and found the best gamma, and therefore quality, on the Mid setting. Also, here are gamma presets and color temps with a set of RGB sliders. There is no color gamut selector, but you can opt for sRGB in the sRGB picture mode.
For panel care, the M10S II includes pixel shift, a screen saver, and refresh routines. Sony differentiates between pixel and panel refresh. I ran the pixel refresh when I first powered up my sample. Selecting panel refresh prompted a message that it should only be run once a year, so I concluded it was a very aggressive refresh routine.
Sony INZONE M10S II Calibration Settings
The M10S II arrived set to its Game mode, which had a cool grayscale and light gamma. I could fix the grayscale but not the gamma, so I turned to Standard mode, which was much better. After a few clicks of the RGB sliders, I had much improved grayscale, gamma, and color tracking. The gamut volume is just under 110% of DCI-P3, which is too large for the SDR standard but looks great, nonetheless. If you want sRGB, it’s there in the preset mode list. It has good gamut accuracy and supports grayscale calibration but not gamma adjustment. My recommended settings are below.
For HDR content, the M10S II switches over automatically and provides four specific picture modes. Game works the best, and I noted that it allowed grayscale calibration and brightness adjustment. You can see those test results on page five.
| Picture Mode | Standard | 
| Brightness 200 nits | 51 | 
| Brightness 120 nits | 28 | 
| Brightness 100 nits | 23 | 
| Brightness 80 nits | 17 | 
| Brightness 50 nits | 8 (min. 22 nits) | 
| Contrast | 75 | 
| Gamma | 2.2 | 
| Color Temp User | Red 100, Green 100, Blue 98 | 
Gaming and Hands-on
Sony’s marketing for the M10S II clearly targets competition and hardcore gamers, and for those users, it delivers. Whether you need 540 Hz or not, it is super quick. Motion resolution is perfect, which means moving objects and backgrounds have the same clarity as stationary elements. Camera pans are free from blur or smearing. Adaptive-Sync worked perfectly for me when using a GeForce RTX 4090 video card. Frame rates in Doom Eternal set to max detail ranged from 350 to 540fps.
The M10S II has a couple of features designed to reduce motion blur and smooth out the image, but I didn’t find any need for them. Anti-flicker, which I’ve seen from Asus as well, is there to remove any flickering during frame rate transitions. I saw plenty of those with rates rapidly shifting 80-100fps by the second. There was no flicker. You also get blur reduction via backlight strobe. It only works below 270 Hz, and since my speeds never went below that, it wasn’t needed. To engage it, turn off Adaptive-Sync first. The M10S II will automatically reduce the refresh rate. It works well and shows no evidence of phasing or ghosting.
Input lag is low enough that I perceived instant response to control inputs during the most frenetic battle maneuvers. My skills are average, but I see this monitor’s benefit to a competitive gamer. The 720 Hz mode felt super quick even though its input lag is only a tad lower. Full-screen resolution is limited to 1280x720, but you can achieve dizzying frame rates in the process. Also available are 24.5-inch modes in which the picture occupies a portion of the screen. You can do 1920x1080 at 720 Hz this way or opt for 2368x1332 pixels in a 1:1 mapping.
In all scenarios, color and clarity are as good as it gets for the OLED genre. The M10S II has a huge color gamut, almost 110% of DCI-P3, and that shows in both SDR and HDR content. HDR has the additional capability of calibration, something most HDR monitors cannot do. I also liked the variable brightness options. The terminology is a little counterintuitive in that when Brightness stabilizer is off, variable brightness is engaged at maximum. The other settings, Mid and High, are less aggressive at modulating light output. I found the best gamma, and therefore picture quality, came from the Mid option.
As a 27-inch QHD flat panel, the M10S II is well suited for productivity and delivers a clean and colorful picture for general use. Small text is sharp and free of color fringing. Graphics and photos are deeply textured, and video looks great as well. The monitor makes a great personal TV. The only things I noted missing were internal speakers and LED lighting. But everything you need for gaming, entertainment, and work is there.
Takeaway: The M10S II is a competitor’s dream with its speedy response, smooth motion resolution, and multitude of refresh and resolution options. It delivers a clean and colorful picture for both SDR and HDR content. The anti-glare layer is among the best I’ve seen, with no effects seen from ambient light reflections. It’s a premium purchase for sure, but there is nothing it cannot do well.
