A flood of quantum shares
Toronto quantum company Xanadu saw its first share lockup lift for a majority of investors yesterday, six months after it went public via a SPAC deal. The stock closed the day down by more than 20 percent, at around $8 CAD, which was a far cry from its peak of nearly $50 CAD in May. CEO Christian Weedbrook told The Globe and Mail that making more shares available will help attract investment in the long term.
Call my agent
The hottest new agentic AI assistants on the block are Instinct (still in private beta) and Meta’s Muse (now available in Canada). These agents can book reservations, send texts on your behalf, and even make online purchases. Shopify is getting in on the action through a partnership that allows Muse to buy from Shopify-powered stores.
A new frontier model
Meanwhile, one of the co-creators of ChatGPT has released Jev, a “new type of foundation model” that he claims is up to hundreds of times faster and cheaper than existing models. Unlike other LLMs, Jev doesn’t generate text; instead, it generates decisions for software (like probabilities and classifications).
Tech giants agree with (non-binding) data centre rules
Canada’s voluntary federal responsible data centre development framework has new additions, including chipmakers Nvidia and AMD, along with US tech giants Intel, IBM, and Lenovo. The framework’s suggestions, which companies aren’t required to follow, include ensuring low environmental impact and water use.
BlackBerry is so back
Canadian tech smartphone-darling-turned-vehicle-software-player is continuing its comeback journey. On Tuesday, BlackBerry announced a contract worth more than $100 million USD to provide its Alloy Kore software platform to Coretura, a joint venture between Volvo Group and Daimler Truck.
BC v. OpenAI
The province of BC has sued OpenAI in California, arguing that the AI company could have averted the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, BC, had it notified Canadian authorities of the alleged shooter’s ChatGPT logs.
OpenAI is already facing dozens of lawsuits from victims and families of the tragedy. The tech company has asked for many of them to be dismissed, and to be tried in BC.
“Astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”
OpenAI is also fighting copyright infringement suits in court, and public court documents have surfaced some unfiltered internal commentary. The US politics magazine Mother Jones’ lawsuit against the AI giant revealed internal discussions about model training, where one Microsoft document warned that many people will consider LLM training to be “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions.”

As AI becomes increasingly involved in software coding, Boast is helping companies build defensible tax claims and navigate how AI-assisted development will reshape their eligible R&D.
On the move
This week’s hires, fires, and exec shakeups:

- Canadian film giant Cineplex named Bill Walker as its new CEO as it embarks on a strategic review and potential sale.

articles.title: Logitech acaba de presentar los únicos tres periféricos que necesitarás para ganar en cualquier juego
articles.text:
Si eres jugador competitivo, o un jugador casual que le gusta usar lo mejor de lo mejor, seguro que te suena la gama Pro X de Logitech G. Dentro del gaming, no solo son los periféricos más usados por los jugadores de alto nivel, sino también los más por aquellos que quieren tener en su escritorio lo mejor que se puede usar en el gaming. Ahora la compañía ha renovado tres de sus productos clave, haciendo lo que ya era tope de gama, mejor.
En particular, la compañía ha presentado la nueva generación del Superstrike 3, su ratón háptico de alto rendimiento que sorprendía a todos hace algún tiempo y que para muchos cambió para siempre la forma de jugar con ratón gracias a su sistema de Respuesta Háptica Inductiva (HITS) y a su sistema de microinterruptores.
Ahora llega la versión PRO X3 SUPERSTRIKE, fruto de la colaboración que mantienen Logitech y los jugadores profesionales que han ayudado a moldear este ratón, haciéndolo mejor que el anterior, algo que ya era difícil. Ahora no solo es un 50 % más eficiente en su consumo energético (lo que se traduce en más batería), sino que también ofrece un chasis más ligero y más equilibrado. Mantiene la tecnología HITS, lo que hace que con el ratón apagado no haya click, puesto que el click real es una sensación háptica.
Mantiene su sobresaliente sensor HERO 2, 1000 HZ de conexión por cable y los 8000 Hz de la conexión Lightspeed; es totalmente personalizable con G Hub y es, en pocas palabras, el mejor ratón que puede comprar para jugar al competitivo (como ya lo era la generación anterior).
Al ratón, como no podía ser de otra forma, lo acompaña el teclado gaming PRO X2 RAPID, que ofrece un salto de calidad enorme dentro del espectro de TKL para el gaming, ofreciendo interruptores magnéticos personalizados, tecnología Rapid Trigger y Key Priority configurable a través de G Hub. Además, se puede controlar usando la pantalla OLED integrada para recalibrar los parámetros al instante en tiempo real.
Nueva generación de sus auriculares Pro X
Y completan el trío la nueva generación de sus auriculares pro: los PRO X3 LIGHTSPEED Gaming Headset son oficiales y mejoran en todo a la generación anterior, unos de los más aclamados del mercado. Ahora incorporan un micrófono de 48 kHz con calidad de estudio, una mayor autonomía y mejoras en los drivers. Además de una de las funciones más esperadas en esta gama: ecualización paramétrica a través de G Hub, que permite personalizar al máximo los auriculares y tener control granular del sonido con perfiles para cada juego de forma independiente... o usar los de la comunidad.
No obstante, las novedades de Logitech no terminan aquí, puesto que, además de su gama Pro, la compañía también ha renovado (y lanzado) un puñado de nuevos productos. Dentro de la gama premium pero más asequible, Logitech ha presentado el G316 X 75, su teclado mecánico, junto a una nueva colección de keycaps, y ha actualizado el sensor de HERO en los G502 X PLUS y G502 X LIGHTSPEED.
Por su parte, también habrá un nuevo color para los ASTRO A50 X, en rojo, llamado Mars Red Edition. Eso sí, ten en cuenta que este nuevo color es exclusivo, como en el caso de McLaren para los X, y no estará disponible en los GEN 5. Y para streamers, hay un nuevo modelo del mítico micrófono, que ahora se llama Yeti 2, e incluye una pantalla para controlar parámetros, un sistema de reducción de ruido basado en IA que aísla la voz frente al entorno e integración directa con G HUB.

articles.title: Spotify’s Taste Profile must’ve been a victory, because it’s finally coming to the US in beta — here are 3 tips that could give your feed the spring cleaning it needs
articles.text:
Spotify is bringing its algorithm-amending Taste Profile tool to listeners in the US, and it could be your one-way ticket to wiping your most-hated genres from your feed
A quick and easy way to train your recommendations
- Taste Profile is expanding to US listeners following a test trial
- It's essentially Spotify's interpretation of your listening habits
- You can interact with Taste Profile directly, telling it what you want and don't want to hear
Spotify’s dedication to creating a complete personalized listening experience is still one of its biggest priorities, and the best music streaming is bringing one of its smartest tools to even more listeners.
After its successful test run in New Zealand, Spotify is taking the next steps by expanding Taste Profile, a feature that allows you to see exactly what Spotify thinks about your music taste and streaming habits. The tool is rolling out today (September 23) in beta for Premium users in the US over the age of 18.
If you’re a Spotify user with beta access, you can find the new Taste Profile tab in the sidebar by tapping on your profile image.
Essentially, Spotify is bringing Taste Profile out of the shadows of the algorithm and into the forefront of the mobile experience, but Spotify’s growing music tool is designed to give you a more robust way of controlling your recommendations.
Not only can you read Spotify’s interpretation of your music taste, you can communicate directly with the algorithm and fine-tune the recommendations that appear on the Home page — so you don’t have to rely solely on your in-app activity to shape music discovery if you don’t want to.
Interested in branching out to a genre you’ve always wanted to explore, but never found the time to? With the Taste Profile prompt box, try typing specific requests like ‘show me more experimental pop’, and your Home feed will adjust accordingly. It also works for finding new artists to add to your radar — I’d suggest using the tool to find emerging artists and give them the streaming boosts they deserve.
Secondly, you can tell Taste Profile what you want to see more of, and what you want to see less of. While you can already remove individual songs from your Taste Profile, this could allow you to remove entire genres from your recommendations. Additionally, you can use Taste Profile to quickly summon tunes that fit your current mood, a handy workaround to finding music that complements a social gathering or personal listening session — but it doesn’t have to be all about the music.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Unlike music discovery, getting started with podcasts can be a bit tricky; at least that’s how I find it anyway. The in-app Podcasts hub is a rich epicenter of shows, but sometimes I feel Spotify bumps the most popular ones in favor of those that explore more niche topics. Podcasts about classic cinema are my thing, and it’s taken me a long time to find shows I feel give me what I’m looking for.
If you feel you’re in a similar boat, Taste Profile could help you. Similar to music prompts, you can tell Taste Profile what topics interest you most, triggering your Home page to feed you suggestions to match. You might already be a huge fan of true crime podcasts, but want to find shows or episodes that explore individual criminals, specific crimes, or the most famous cases from certain historical periods.
For seasoned users, most of the hard work and fine-tuning of the algorithm has already been done. Thanks to years' worth of non-stop listening, creating playlists, and using existing tools such as 'Don't play this artist' to help Spotify understand me, I'm confident that I don't need to do any further tweaking. That being said, if you've just made the switch to Spotify or AI-generated music is infiltrating your recommendations, it could be a game-changer.

articles.title: Upgrade your gaming experience with this 27-inch Acer 1440p 270Hz panel that’s an incredible 45% off — just $179 buys an awesome IPS monitor with AMD FreeSync Premium and 1ms response time
articles.text:
Upgrade your gaming experience with this 27-inch Acer 1440p 270Hz panel that’s an incredible 45% off — just $179 buys an awesome IPS monitor with AMD FreeSync Premium and 1ms response time
Lowest price in the last 90 days for the Acer XV270U and a worthwhile upgrade from 1080p
While RAM, video cards, and storage have become the most expensive parts of a PC build or upgrade, monitors haven’t really flinched price-wise. They can still offer a tangible upgrade, whether for gaming or productivity, for your PC. After all, you are staring at it the entire time you use your PC. Acer is currently offering an incredible deal on the Nitro (XV270U). articles.title: How One Kubernetes YAML Can Hand Over a GCP Organization
articles.text:
When a developer needs to create a cloud resource — a database, a storage bucket, or a virtual machine — they need credentials to authenticate to the cloud provider. In Google Cloud, that often means a service account key: a JSON file that proves who they are and what they're allowed to do.
The problem with service account keys is that they're files. Files get copied, emailed, accidentally committed to Git repositories, left on laptops, and forgotten.
When someone leaves a team, the organization doesn't always know which keys they had. Tracking and rotating credentials across dozens of developers becomes a significant operational burden and security risk.
The industry term for this is secret sprawl: cloud credentials scattered across machines, pipelines, and codebases in ways that are difficult to audit and even harder to remove.
How GitOps removed the credentials
The Kubernetes community's solution to this is a GitOps operator (also known as a controller):
- A developer writes YAML configuration files describing the resources they need, commits them to Git, and applies them to a Kubernetes cluster.
- A controller running inside the cluster reads those files and creates or updates the cloud resources on the developer's behalf.
The key point: developers end up with no cloud credentials at all. The controller authenticates on their behalf, using its own.
Google's version of this system is Google Kubernetes Config Connector (KCC), which typically runs inside a Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) cluster. KCC watches for configuration files describing Google Cloud resources and calls the corresponding Google Cloud API to create or update them.
A developer who wants to grant an application permission to read objects from a storage bucket could submit an IAMPolicyMember resource:
apiVersion: iam.cnrm.cloud.google.com/v1beta1
kind: IAMPolicyMember
metadata:
  name: my-binding
  namespace: my-team
spec:
  member: "serviceAccount:my-app@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com"
  role: roles/storage.objectViewer
  resourceRef:
    kind: Project
    external: "my-project"
KCC authenticates to Google Cloud through Workload Identity, using a Google service account controlled by the platform team — often called the KCC GSA. Because KCC may manage infrastructure across multiple projects, folders, or an entire organization, this account can be given broad roles such as role/owner or roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin.
When the developer submits the resource, KCC picks it up and calls Google Cloud IAM. The permission is created, and the developer never touches a Google Cloud credential.
This setup works well for its intended purpose: no developer credentials, everything declared in Git, and one service account for the platform team to control instead of dozens. The credential sprawl problem is solved.
Continue your journey to reduce data risk at your company
Listen to State of Cybercrime, Varonis’ monthly podcast to learn about high-profile cyberattacks, shadow IT, supply chain incidents, and AI security risks.
Subscribe to the series and catch every future episode.
Subscribe: State of Cybercrime
When namespace access becomes an organization owner
The same setup, however, creates a new problem.
KCC performs every Google Cloud operation through its own service account, regardless of which Kubernetes user submitted the resource. If that account has organization-level permissions, a user with limited cluster access can exercise those permissions indirectly. This technique is called ConfigConfusion, discovered by security researcher Justin O'Leary.
If an attacker has:
- Access to a Kubernetes namespace watched by KCC.
- Permission to create IAMPolicyMember resources in that namespace.
- No Google Cloud credentials or permissions of their own.
They can grant themselves any Google Cloud IAM role that KCC's service account is permitted to assign — including roles/owner on the entire organization.
The attack itself is one command:
apiVersion: iam.cnrm.cloud.google.com/v1beta1
kind: IAMPolicyMember
metadata:
 name: escalation
 namespace: my-team
spec:
 member: "serviceAccount:attacker@attacker-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com"
 role: roles/owner
 resourceRef:
 apiVersion: resourcemanager.cnrm.cloud.google.com/v1beta1
 kind: Organization
 external: "123456789"
The attacker applies the YAML through Kubernetes. KCC reads it and requests the IAM change from Google Cloud using its own service account, which has permission to make it, so the request is accepted. The attacker now controls the Google Cloud organization — without ever holding a Google Cloud credential.
Two authorization systems, one missing check
To understand why this works, look at the two separate authorization systems handling the request.
- Kubernetes RBAC controls what a user can do inside the cluster. It asks: "Is this user allowed to create an IAMPolicyMember resource in this namespace?" If yes, it allows the operation. It knows nothing about Google Cloud and doesn't ask what the resource will do there.
- Google Cloud IAM controls what a service account can do in Google Cloud. When KCC calls Google Cloud to create the binding, it asks: "Does KCC's service account have permission to set this IAM binding?" If yes, it allows the operation. Google Cloud doesn't know which Kubernetes user triggered the request, and doesn't check whether that user should have been allowed to request it.
As a result, Kubernetes only sees the resource being created inside the cluster, and Google Cloud only sees KCC's service account making the change. KCC can receive a request from a user with limited access and carry it out using permissions that user doesn't have in Google Cloud.
This is known as a confused deputy problem: KCC has broad authority and acts on instructions from users with less authority, without checking whether they should be able to use it.
The design decision that removes cloud credentials from developers is useful and intentional. But it also removes the link between a developer's Kubernetes identity and the Google Cloud permissions used on their behalf. When KCC acts, Google Cloud sees KCC — not the person who triggered the request.
Google calls it a feature
Google's response to ConfigConfusion was that KCC is working as designed.
The administrator chose to give KCC an organization-level service account, and chose to allow developers to create IAMPolicyMember resources in KCC-managed namespaces. From Google's perspective, those are configuration decisions, and KCC carries out the request it was given.
That explanation is technically accurate, and KCC does exactly what it's configured to do.
The issue is that the documentation doesn't make the relationship between these two decisions obvious. Most administrators think about them separately: which Kubernetes resource types can this team create, and what can KCC's service account do in Google Cloud? In KCC, the two are connected — giving a team permission to create an IAMPolicyMember resource can also give that team a way to use KCC's Google Cloud authority.
Working out the exact permissions KCC needs is difficult, so granting organization-level access is often easier. It doesn't necessarily reflect poor administration — it's the natural outcome of a design that doesn't make the resulting authority gap visible.
Why it's hard to fix
The most obvious fix would be to check whether the Kubernetes user who submitted a resource has the corresponding Google Cloud permission before carrying out the request.
That check depends on the Kubernetes user having a Google Cloud identity — but KCC is designed so that they don't need one. Giving each user a corresponding identity would undermine the model KCC was built to provide, while looking up the requester's permissions for every resource would add an authorization check and extra API calls to every reconciliation cycle.
Google's recommended mitigations therefore focus on reducing the authority available through KCC, rather than changing how it authorizes each request.
The same risk in AWS and Azure
The authorization problem isn't unique to KCC. Any infrastructure operator that accepts instructions from one identity and carries them out through another can create the same gap. What changes between platforms is how much authority the operator holds and how easily that authority can be limited.
- AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK) separates controllers by service. IAM, Amazon S3, and Amazon EC2 each have their own controller, with an IAM role scoped to that service. If a user gains control of the S3 controller's request path, they can affect S3 resources but can't make IAM changes, because its role doesn't have those permissions.
- Azure Service Operator v2 allows each Kubernetes namespace to use a separate managed identity. This gives administrators a practical way to limit permissions per namespace, rather than placing the entire operator's authority behind one identity.
Neither approach removes the underlying confused deputy risk, but both reduce the potential damage by limiting the operator's permissions before a malicious request reaches it.
How to secure Config Connector
To reduce this risk, you need to limit both sides of the authorization gap: what KCC's service account can do in Google Cloud, and which Kubernetes users can submit resources for it to process.
The checklist below covers both sides.
- Does KCC use namespaced mode, with a separately scoped Google service account for each namespace?
- Have you reviewed KCC's IAM roles at the project, folder, and organization levels?
- Have broad roles such as roles/owner and roles/resourcemanager.organizationAdmin been removed unless they are strictly required?
- Is permission to create IAMPolicyMember, IAMPolicy, and IAMPartialPolicy resources limited to approved platform or infrastructure teams?
- Do you monitor folder and organization-level IAM changes made by KCC, particularly those outside the approved GitOps workflow?
The vulnerable configuration combines a KCC service account with organization-level IAM permissions and broad write access to KCC-managed namespaces.
Either condition can be managed on its own, but together they create a privilege-escalation path that requires no Google Cloud credentials to exploit.

articles.title: Meta's Muse AI calls businesses for you, sometimes with a human doing the talking
articles.text:
Cutting corners: Meta wants Muse to take everyday chores off your hands, but some of that AI has involved actual people. The company has been testing a human concierge service that lets contractors handle calls for its new personal AI agent, raising privacy concerns among its own employees.
According to Reuters, the experiment was enabled for half of Meta's employees last week, with an opt-out group available. Staff warned that sensitive information could end up with call-center contractors. A Meta executive acknowledged that introducing human operators without clear disclosure was a mistake, and the human concierge feature has been rolled back for now.
There was also an incident that highlighted another potential problem with handing the calls to humans. One employee who asked Muse to call an internet and cable provider to negotiate his bill said a transcript showed that the contractor had made a racist reference during the call. Meta apologized to the employee and said the human agent involved would not work on any of its projects again.
Muse's separate phone-calling feature allows users to contact US businesses for tasks such as booking haircuts or checking whether an item is in stock.
 – Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) September 16, 2026
Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said employee feedback had been largely positive. He added that the company would only release the potential feature publicly once it was ready, with appropriate disclosures and safeguards.
Launched on September 8, Muse is Meta's attempt to turn the chatbot into something closer to a personal assistant. Users can interact with it through its own app or WhatsApp, asking it to send emails, arrange travel, and work toward longer-term goals.
Meta says the agent runs inside a dedicated virtual machine, with a separate Sentinel agent checking outgoing actions. Users control connected services and approve sensitive steps, including purchases. The company also says conversations and data stored in that virtual machine are kept out of its advertising systems.
Meta's own testing suggests why it is experimenting with humans in the first place. Some businesses simply hang up on Muse when they realize they are talking to an AI, which is no surprise. Internal tests found that handing calls to human agents could increase the success rate to between 95% and 98%, compared with a much lower rate for calls handled entirely by AI.
There have been plenty of examples of supposedly automated services relying heavily on humans behind the scenes. One of the most memorable was shopping app Nate, which claimed AI could automatically complete online purchases. According to the Department of Justice, hundreds of workers in call centers in the Philippines and Romania were actually completing many of the transactions manually. Sources previously claimed that between 60% and 100% of purchases were handled this way during parts of 2021.
Amazon's "Just Walk Out" stores offered another example. The supposedly cashierless technology relied on more than 1,000 workers in India to review transactions and label footage. It was reported that around 700 out of every 1,000 purchases required human review as of 2022, although Amazon disputed those figures.
In 2023, Presto Automation revealed that around 70% of orders handled by its AI drive-thru system required intervention from off-site human agents, including workers in the Philippines.
Meta's been here before with Facebook M, the digital concierge launched in closed beta during the summer of 2015 and shut down a few years later. Every message the service fielded was reviewed by contractors who worked at the company's Menlo Park headquarters, but at launch, Facebook said the service was powered by AI trained and supervised by real people.
For its part, Meta is openly testing human assistance rather than claiming that contractors do not exist. But if a feature is marketed as an AI making calls on your behalf, users will probably want to know when the person actually doing the talking is sitting in a call center.

articles.title: Grâce à 2 panneaux solaires, cette montre Amazfit promet une autonomie record
articles.text:
Après la T-Rex Ultra 2, Amazfit dévoile une nouvelle variante de son célèbre modèle, à savoir la T-Rex Dual Solar. Comme son nom l’indique, cette nouvelle montre connectée est équipée de deux panneaux solaires : l’un intégré à l’avant de la montre, l’autre situé sur le boîtier arrière. Grâce à ce dispositif, Amazfit annonce une autonomie record pour son nouveau modèle. Par ailleurs, la T-Rex Dual Solar se destine résolument aux aventuriers, avec notamment une lampe torche intégrée et un mode SOS.
Autonomie record et 2 modes de recharge
L’Amazfit T-Rex Dual Solar est équipée de deux petits panneaux solaires. Le premier est situé dans l’écran, tandis que le second, deux fois plus grand, est positionné dans le boîtier arrière. Ainsi, deux modes de recharge sont possibles : lorsque la montre connectée est portée au poignet ou lorsque le boîtier arrière est orienté face au soleil, lors d’une pause par exemple. Au passage, étant donné que le panneau solaire est situé dans le boîtier arrière, la recharge est deux fois plus rapide que celle proposée par le panneau intégré dans l’écran de la montre. Il faut néanmoins enlever la montre et la placer au soleil pour pouvoir bénéficier de cette recharge deux fois plus rapide.
Vous l’aurez compris, cette montre est destinée aux randonnées de très longues distances ou aux périples sportifs qui peuvent s’étaler sur plusieurs jours. Justement, Amazfit annonce une autonomie record pour cette montre connectée équipée de panneaux solaires. À titre d’exemple, selon Amazfit, l’autonomie de cette montre pourrait atteindre 34 jours en utilisation normale, grâce à son panneau solaire intégré à l’écran, exposé trois heures par jour à une luminosité de 50 000 nits. Dans le cadre d’une utilisation intensive, l’autonomie serait de 18 jours, grâce à son panneau solaire intégré à l’arrière du boîtier, exposé trois heures par jour à une luminosité de 50 000 nits.
Écran AMOLED, lampe torche intégrée et mode SOS
En parallèle de ses deux panneaux solaires et de ses promesses d’autonomie record, nous pouvons aussi noter que la montre présente un écran AMOLED de 1,32 pouce, dont la luminosité peut atteindre jusqu’à 3 000 nits. L’écran est quant à lui protégé par un verre saphir résistant aux rayures et aux chocs.
La T-Rex Dual Solar présente par ailleurs un panneau arrière en verre céramique, ainsi qu’une lunette et quatre boutons en titane Grade 5. Elle s’annonce donc particulièrement robuste. Elle aurait d’ailleurs été conçue pour fonctionner dans des températures comprises entre -30 °C et +70 °C et elle intègre une lampe torche LED réglable jusqu’à 300 lux, ainsi qu’un mode SOS.
Enfin, notons que cette montre propose une navigation étape par étape grâce à six systèmes satellitaires, dont le GPS et Galileo. Elle permet également de télécharger des cartes couleur, topographiques et de pistes de ski, tout en affichant le profil d’altitude et les points de cheminement. Côté santé, elle assure le suivi de la fréquence cardiaque, de la saturation en oxygène dans le sang et de certains indicateurs de fatigue. La version européenne prend également en charge les paiements NFC.
La T-Rex Dual Solar est disponible dès à présent sur les sites en ligne européens d’Amazfit au prix de vente conseillé de 649,90 euros.

articles.title: Microsoft’s new Surface Mouse has haptic feedback and a customizable action button
articles.text:
Microsoft is launching a second generation of its Surface Mouse next month that includes haptic feedback support. The Surface Mouse also has a customizable action button for the first time, which is primarily designed for quick access to Copilot (of course), but can be configured to work with other shortcuts from the Surface app.
Microsoft’s new Surface Mouse has haptic feedback and a customizable action button
The $79.99 Surface Mouse will start shipping on October 13th.
“Its haptic feedback adds a small, purposeful physical response to the moment you usually only see on a screen: a click registering, a window snapping into place or an object aligning just right,” says Brett Ostrum, corporate vice president of Surface Devices. “It is subtle by design, but noticeable within seconds — and hard to give up once you have it.”
The haptic feedback works with things like clicks, drags, and alignment throughout Windows 11, but the tactile feedback also triggers in apps like PowerPoint, Affinity, Concepts, and Filmora. Microsoft added support for haptic feedback in Windows 11 earlier this year, and so far it’s mainly Microsoft and Logitech that are supporting it with dedicated hardware. Logitech’s MX Master 4 has haptic feedback, and its Pro X2 Superstrike (and today’s new X3) includes a haptic-based clicks system that doesn’t support the Windows 11 haptic feedback. The upcoming Surface Laptop Ultra also has a haptic trackpad.
After originally launching the Surface Mouse in 2016 and not updating it since, Microsoft has now redesigned it to be more comfortable for all-day use, with a soft-touch material at the top. Thanks to Bluetooth 6.0 support, you can now also pair it with up to three devices.
The new Surface Mouse will be available on October 13th, the same day Microsoft launches its refreshed Surface Pro 12-inch and Surface Laptop 13-inch devices. It will be priced at $79.99, and available in black and platinum color options.

articles.title: YouTube is making comments more fun — and fandom more lucrative for creators | TechCrunch
articles.text:
YouTube’s comments section is getting an upgrade, alongside the rollout of other community-focused features such as exclusive paid memberships, the company announced at its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday. Commenters will now be able to respond with GIFs or leave comments from their TVs, while creators will get new tools to support their fan communities, including features to personalize moderation, invite members into VIP-like areas, and give fans new ways to help them make money from their content.
Comments are still one of the main ways YouTube viewers interact with creators’ content, but they’ve often lagged behind other social networks’ commenting features. For instance, TikTok just announced that commenters can respond to videos with their voice and add polls, photo carousels, and Live Photos to their comments. Spotify lets video podcasters use polls and Q&As to engage their audiences.
YouTube is finally catching up a bit by adding support for leaving GIFs in comments and letting users comment while watching YouTube on TV. The latter works by voice, not painfully typing out “LOL” on your remote control, YouTube noted.
One of the more interesting additions is a new comment moderation tool that’s personalized to each creator’s needs. Though YouTube already offers a comment moderation filter, creators may want to tailor it more precisely, particularly on live videos, where it’s harder to keep up. For now, the company is calling this personalized moderation an “experiment” and didn’t provide specific technical details about how it works.
Other features are meant to help creators grow their fan communities — and make money from that fandom. These arrive at a time when revenue from advertising is no longer the only way creators monetize their videos.
The company said its Channel Memberships features are evolving, with the addition of paid, members-only communities, where members can share posts and start discussions with other top fans. YouTube will market these communities alongside other memberships on a new “channel memberships” page for viewers, designed to help them discover ones that match their interests.
Hype, a feature that lets fans recommend smaller creators’ videos to others and climb fan leaderboards, will gain new functionality dubbed “Hype with Jewels.” Previously, fans could only “hype” videos three times per week for free. Now they can buy Jewels, a virtual currency of sorts, to hype videos even more, helping to support creators and grow their audience. Fans motivated by clout may also appreciate that their handles will be permanently added to the video’s description.
YouTube said viewers have so far hyped more than 75 million unique videos over 1 billion times.
The company’s direct messaging feature for sharing videos with family and friends will also support group chats in the next few months. Users will be able to record quick, raw videos and share them in these conversations, too.
These community-focused features arrived alongside other creator tools, including those for A/B testing, live dubbing, AI-assisted video editing, and more.

articles.title: Ghana’s Complete Farmer secures $2.4m convertible loan from IFC - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ghanaian agri-tech startup Complete Farmer has secured a US$2.4 million convertible loan from the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to scale up and finance inputs and agronomy services for farmers, complemented by US$480,000 in advisory to strengthen its systems and capacity to expand farmer financing.
Founded in 2017, Complete Farmer is an agricultural trading company connecting international commodity buyers with smallholder farmers across Ghana and Togo. The company works with more than 72,000 farmers and supplies international buyers, including Aldi and Lidl, and its operations are supported by more than 350 field agents and eight fulfillment centres responsible for aggregation, grading, quality control and export logistics.
The startup has expanded beyond agricultural trading, developing a marketplace for farm inputs and equipment and a credit product that uses farm data to help farmers access financing.
Complete Farmer raised US$10.4 million in pre-Series A funding back in September 2023, and last year banked US$2.5 million from the European Union-funded AgriFI facility to boost its expansion efforts. It has now secured further capital from the IFC, with support from the Business Investment Financing Track (BIFT) of the GAFSP, to help it connect more smallholder farmers with financial institutions. The partnership is expected to expand and provide support to 240,000 farmers, including facilitating access to finance by 2030.
“For us, this partnership is about making finance work better for farmers,” said Desmond Koney, CEO of Complete Farmer.
“Too many farmers with the capacity to grow commercially still struggle to access the financing they need to do so. Over the years, we have focused on building the technology, data and market infrastructure that makes it possible to better understand farmers, support their production and connect what they grow to real demand. Our partnership with IFC allows us to build on that foundation and scale our input financing model, so that more farmers have the resources and support they need to grow sustainably and participate more meaningfully in agricultural markets.”

articles.title: Test de l'iPhone 18 Pro : le meilleur iPhone est aussi le plus prudent — Frandroid
articles.text:
Après mon test de l’iPhone 17 Pro, voici, un an plus tard, celui du 18 Pro. Et pourtant, j’ai passé l’année avec un Air au final, que je n’avais pas testé à l’époque. J’étais trop attiré par la nouveauté, mais les compromis de l’Air ont fini par me lasser. Il faut dire que je fais 1,7 charge par jour actuellement. En gros, je charge presque deux fois mon smartphone par jour, ce n’est plus tenable.
Bref, retour au Pro. Et le 18 Pro arrive avec 150 euros de hausse, sans iPhone 18 standard à côté de lui, et avec une nouveauté photo dont tout le monde a compris qu’elle était plus impressionnante à annoncer qu’à utiliser. Cela ne nous a pas empêchés de le tester à fond.
Petite mise au point avant de commencer : on n’est pas là pour faire du Apple bashing, mais on ne va pas non plus verser dans l’éloge aveugle à coups de superlatifs. Ce n’a jamais été notre genre. L’iPhone Pro excelle sur bien des points et bute encore sur d’autres, et on va vous expliquer lesquels.
Fiche technique

| Puce | Apple A20 Pro (2 nm) : CPU 6 cœurs (2 super cœurs + 4 cœurs efficacité), GPU 7 cœurs avec Neural Accelerators et ray tracing matériel, deux Neural Engine 16 cœurs (32 cœurs au total) |  | 
| Mémoire vive | 12 Go (non communiqué par Apple, relevé dans Xcode) |  | 
| Stockage | 256 Go, 512 Go, 1 To, 2 To |  | 
| Caméra principale | Fusion 48 MP, 24 mm, ouverture variable ƒ/1,48 – ƒ/1,8 – ƒ/2,8 – ƒ/4,0, stabilisation par déplacement du capteur 2ᵉ génération, 100 % Focus Pixels, 2x « qualité optique » 12 MP (48 mm) |  |
