articles.title: Claude Opus 5.5 face à GPT-6 Sol et Luna : trois nouvelles IA d'un coup, et des prix qui chutent
articles.text:
Claude Opus 5.5 face à GPT-6 Sol et Luna : trois nouvelles IA d'un coup, et des prix qui chutent
Ralentir la course à l'IA, première étape : lancer un nouveau modèle
Le 12 septembre, le patron d'Anthropic appelait l'industrie à lever le pied. Ce mardi 22 septembre, la société dégaine Claude Opus 5.5, moins cher et plus rapide, et OpenAI réplique quatre-vingt-dix minutes plus tard avec GPT-6 Sol et Luna, à prix cassés.
Il y a dix jours, Dario Amodei publiait sur son site un long essai consacré à la vitesse de développement de l'IA. Le PDG d'Anthropic exhortait la poignée de laboratoires installés à la pointe de l'IA à modérer ensemble la cadence de leurs progrès, le temps que la sécurité rattrape la puissance.
	
Nous devons ralentir le rythme auquel nous améliorons les capacités des modèles d'IA. Le progrès semblera toujours rapide.
Amodei précisait que cette modération n'impliquait aucun gel de l'entraînement des modèles.
Claude Opus 5.5 : plus rapide, moins cher, testé par des évaluateurs externes
Ce mardi 22 septembre, Anthropic a dévoilé Claude Opus 5.5, qu'il présente comme sa première sortie depuis cet appel. Le modèle a été éprouvé avant publication par des évaluateurs externes, dont METR et Frontier Design. L'éditeur revendique un niveau comparable à Claude Fable 5.1 sur la plupart des tâches et affirme devancer GPT-6 Astra sur plusieurs bancs d'essai, parmi lesquels Terminal-Bench 4.0 et Humanity's Last Exam.
Le tarif baisse : 4 dollars le million de tokens en entrée et 20 en sortie, contre 5 et 25 pour Opus 5. En y ajoutant une consommation de tokens plus sobre, Anthropic chiffre l'économie à 40 % sur les usages courants.
GPT-6 Sol et Luna : OpenAI annonce ses nouveaux modèles le même jour
Quatre-vingt-dix minutes plus tard, OpenAI présentait GPT-6 Sol et Luna, déclinaisons allégées de son modèle phare GPT-6 Astra. Sol cible le code complexe et les agents autonomes, Luna les tâches répétitives à gros volume. Comptez 2 et 10 dollars le million de tokens pour le premier, 0,10 et 0,50 dollar pour le second. La réduction de moitié annoncée se calcule à partir des prix promotionnels de GPT-5.6 Sol ; la grille officielle de juillet fixait ce dernier à 5 et 30 dollars.
Les deux modèles se déploient progressivement chez les abonnés Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise et Edu, tandis que les inscrits des formules Free et Go accèdent à Luna via l'application desktop.
En une matinée, les deux principaux rivaux de l'IA générative ont donc renouvelé leur gamme et révisé leurs tarifs à la baisse, dix jours après la publication de l'essai d'Amodei.

articles.title: Honeywell: OT Security Teams Embrace AI, but Autonomy Still Rare
articles.text:
Honeywell released its 2026 OT Cybersecurity Benchmark Report on Tuesday, and the findings point to a disconnect between how industrial organizations rate their operational technology (OT) security programs and how prepared they actually are. The report also examines AI’s impact on OT security.
Among 603 surveyed leaders across critical infrastructure sectors, 88% characterized their OT security programs as mature or design-led, yet only 21% maintain a complete inventory of their OT assets.
Respondents worked across critical infrastructure sectors, including energy, oil and gas, healthcare, maritime, and manufacturing, with participation spanning the Americas, EMEA and APAC regions.
Visibility gaps showed up in monitoring as well as inventory. Just 33% of respondents said OT is fully integrated into a centralized security operations center, and only 20% continuously monitor more than three-quarters of connected IoT devices.
Organizations that experienced a significant OT cybersecurity incident reported an average of 16.2 hours of downtime. Among incident-affected respondents, 21% estimated downtime costs above $100,000 per hour, and 4% put losses above $500,000 per hour.
Incident rates varied sharply by sector. Ninety-one percent of energy and utilities respondents and 87% of maritime respondents reported a significant OT cybersecurity incident in the past 12 months, compared with 54% of oil and gas respondents.
In healthcare, only 19% of respondents said facility and building systems are fully integrated into cybersecurity monitoring and protection.
As for AI, 99% of respondents expect it to affect OT security operations within the next 2-3 years.
AI-enabled tools are already common across OT security functions, with 72% of respondents using AI for threat detection, 68% for continuous monitoring, and 59% for asset inventory.
Hands-On Cyber-Physical Systems Training at ICS Cybersecurity Conference
Still, just 23% currently use autonomous or agentic AI for threat detection, suggesting most deployments so far support human analysts rather than act on their own.
“As AI moves from assisting analysts toward taking action, organizations will need clear decision rights, human oversight and testing that accounts for the operational consequences of an incorrect response,” Honeywell said in its report. “The goal of well-governed AI automation is to strengthen visibility and response without creating new risks to uptime, equipment or safety.”

articles.title: Modular Edge Computing at Multi-Tenant SaaS Scale on Cloudflare Workers
Nrth Festival’s inaugural opening night was a prompt to bring human control back to tech | BetaKit
articles.text:
As Elevate evolved into something new this year, opening night speakers for the newly crowned Nrth Festival wrestled with how to take back control of a world that’s done the same.
Many of Kids Help Phone’s text interactions with kids now start with “are you even a real human?”
At the kickoff event inside Toronto’s Meridian Hall on Tuesday evening, the audience learned they were no longer at the ninth-annual Elevate Festival; instead, they were at the first-ever Nrth Festival. Elevate board member Arlene Dickinson said attendees, many of whom were crunching on complimentary popcorn, should look to their “North stars” to build something that can “stand what’s going on in the world, collectively.”
“What I see with Nrth is this real ground in who we are culturally, and what innovation can mean for our country, and what the future can be in terms of being bright and full of opportunity for all of the citizens that are living here,” Dickinson said.
As might be expected in 2026, innovation is often a pseudonym for AI, and this year’s stage conversations tackled “AI, a little more AI, a little more AI, then basketball,” event host Amber Mac quipped, referencing the event’s concluding speaker: Toronto Raptors legend Kyle Lowry.
While last year’s opening night conversations broadly centred on how AI will change the world and labour, tech leaders this year reckoned with the reality AI has actually created: a lack of human control.
RELATED: Elevate transforms into Nrth Festival in opening-night rebrand
François Chadwick, CFO of Canada’s frontier AI developer, Cohere, shared his own uncertainty in a conversation with TD executive vice-president Rizwan Khalfan. While discussing responsible enterprise AI adoption and the two firms’ new partnership, Chadwick said he recently dropped his child off in New York for school and wondered, when will AI change all of this for him?
“It’s constant training and critical thinking,” Chadwick said. “We’ve got to keep that training going for all folks to make sure as AI continues to adopt and adapt that we bring everybody along.”
Khalfan agreed, adding that the principle guiding the tech should be “AI first, human always.”
“If there’s one thing we can leave you with, then that’s it,” Khalfan added.
The lack of control youth have over tech was underscored by Kids Help Phone executive vice-president Justin Scaini and his colleague Tamar Brannigan. Following up on Scaini’s appearance at last year’s event, which ran through how tech is creeping into Canada’s youth mental health crisis, the duo highlighted a 13-year-old who texted their organization for support because they felt that more of their life was being outsourced to tech solutions that “just didn’t work for them.” More broadly, they noted that many of their organization’s text interactions with kids start with “are you even a real human?”
Brannigan said Kids Help Phone is working with youth to identify the “modern anatomy” of an online safe space. So far, that anatomy includes the “head” guiding transparent data collection, the “heart” interrogating whether a business incentive is genuinely in the best interests of a younger person’s well-being or safety, and the “lungs” as an organization actually following through on what it says it will do. Brannigan said when all three principles are present, young people can be vulnerable, get support, and be kept safe.
“Technology can help open the door, but human connection must be what safely carries them through it,” Brannigan said.
RELATED: How the future of tech and Canada’s sovereignty are changing Elevate
Of course, the best way for data to be kept safe is to not collect it in the first place, DuckDuckGo CPO Beah Burger-Lenehan noted in a conversation with Mac. The privacy-focused search engine and AI platform has carved its place in the market by not collecting use data, instead giving people control over how much AI they want in their search experience, if at all. But in a night that broadly celebrated Canadian approaches to technology, Burger-Lenehan warned that the looming Lawful Access Act, which would give law enforcement more power to monitor and collect personal communications and data, may take control out of Canadian hands.
“If this was passed as written, we might have to pull our VPN from Canada rather than betray our users, really, and break our privacy promise,” Burger-Lenehan said. “Which would be a shame, because policy should protect people and not put them into this difficult trade-off.”
The evening closed on a note of optimism dressed in Toronto Tempo purple, as Lowry—a six-time NBA All-Star who couldn’t stop the Nrth attendees from cheering if he tried—recounted the Raptors’ 2019 championship run and his love for the city of Toronto. Addressing the entrepreneurs in the room, Lowry urged the attendees to believe in themselves and the time they put into their craft, even if they don’t know when or where it will pay off.
“Don’t stop just because [you] got one no,” Lowry said. “It might be 400 no’s, but it’s that one yes, that one opportunity that takes it to the next level.”
The crowd sent The Great Raptor of All Time off with a standing ovation.
With files from Josh Scott.
BetaKit is an Nrth media partner. Feature image courtesy Nrth.

articles.title: Paramount avalia receber investimento de Elon Musk enquanto se prepara para concluir aquisição da Warner
articles.text:
A Paramount está avaliando a possibilidade de convidar Elon Musk para participar do grupo de investidores que ajudará a financiar a aquisição da Warner Bros. Discovery. A informação foi divulgada pelo Semafor nesta quarta-feira (23), com base em pessoas familiarizadas com as discussões.
Musk seria um entre vários indivíduos ricos considerados pelo CEO da Paramount, David Ellison, para integrar um sindicato de investidores de capital da empresa.
Até o momento, porém, não há confirmação de que Musk tenha aceitado participar do negócio. O valor de um eventual investimento também não foi determinado. A Paramount não comentou a informação, enquanto Musk não respondeu aos pedidos de manifestação feitos pelo Semafor.
A movimentação acontece enquanto a Paramount se prepara para concluir a aquisição da Warner Bros. Discovery, operação avaliada em cerca de US$ 110 bilhões (R$ 580 bilhões).
Por que Elon Musk entrou na conversa?
- A possível aproximação tem uma conexão financeira anterior entre Musk e a família Ellison;
- Larry Ellison, fundador da Oracle e pai de David Ellison, investiu US$ 1 bilhão (R$ 5,3 bilhões) na operação de US$ 44 bilhões (R$ 232 bilhões) que levou Musk a fechar o capital do Twitter, atual X, em 2022;
- Ellison também investiu na Tesla em 2018 e posteriormente integrou o conselho de administração da montadora;
- Agora, é o próprio Larry Ellison quem sustenta uma parcela significativa do financiamento da aquisição da Warner Bros. pela Paramount. Segundo o Semafor, ele garantiu pessoalmente mais de US$ 40 bilhões (R$ 211 bilhões) em recursos destinados à operação;
- A entrada de novos investidores ajudaria a diversificar a base de acionistas e reduzir a exposição financeira da família Ellison no negócio.
Paramount busca novos investidores
Musk não seria o único nome avaliado. Segundo o Semafor, David Ellison considera vários indivíduos com grandes fortunas para formar o sindicato de investidores.
A estrutura financeira da aquisição já envolve diferentes fontes de capital. A operação conta com aproximadamente US$ 47 bilhões (R$ 248 bilhões) em financiamento de capital, além de US$ 54 bilhões (R$ 285 bilhões) em financiamento de dívida.
Entre os investidores estão fundos soberanos da Arábia Saudita, Catar e Emirados Árabes Unidos, além do LionTree Investment Fund. Esses investidores não terão assentos no conselho nem direitos de governança, de acordo com os termos divulgados sobre a estrutura financeira.
A FCC, órgão regulador de telecomunicações dos Estados Unidos, aprovou em setembro a possibilidade de investidores estrangeiros deterem participação indireta na Paramount, desde que não tenham ações com direito a voto nem influência sobre decisões editoriais ou administrativas da empresa.
Leia mais:
- Reino Unido aprova compra bilionária da Warner pela Paramount e impõe condições
- Paramount: donos vendem rede de cinemas UCI no Brasil
- Paramount discute investimento de R$ 8,1 bilhões para salvar megafusão com a Warner
O que Musk poderia passar a controlar?
Caso o investimento avance e a aquisição da Warner Bros. seja concluída, Musk passaria a ter uma participação econômica na empresa que reunirá um enorme portfólio de ativos de entretenimento e mídia.
A combinação colocará sob a mesma companhia propriedades da Paramount e da Warner Bros. Discovery, incluindo operações de cinema, televisão e streaming.
Entre os ativos de notícias estão CBS News e CNN, o que torna a eventual entrada de Musk particularmente relevante por causa de sua atuação no X.
O Semafor observa que uma participação de Musk provavelmente provocaria discussões em Washington sobre a presença de um dos principais acionistas da empresa também no controle de uma plataforma de mídia social. A publicação ressalta, entretanto, que seria improvável que ele tivesse participação formal nas decisões operacionais da companhia.
Aquisição da Warner Bros. entra na reta final
A possível busca por novos investidores ocorre enquanto a Paramount avança para concluir a aquisição da Warner Bros. Discovery.
Nesta semana, a empresa chegou a um acordo com um grupo de procuradores-gerais estaduais dos Estados Unidos que contestava a operação. O acordo removeu um dos principais obstáculos jurídicos ao negócio.
A estrutura da operação ainda depende de etapas relacionadas à conclusão do acordo e ao financiamento. A Paramount também estabeleceu compromissos relacionados à produção cinematográfica e à independência editorial de CBS e CNN como parte dos acordos para avançar com a transação.
Nesse cenário, a possível entrada de Musk representa mais uma alternativa de capital para uma operação que envolve dezenas de bilhões de dólares.
Por enquanto, contudo, Musk é apenas um dos potenciais investidores considerados pela Paramount. Não há confirmação de aporte, participação societária ou valor definido para um eventual investimento.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Anthropic’s biolab made a discovery it’s comparing to Crispr
articles.text:
Anthropic says its AI Claude has “autonomously discovered” a new enzyme system similar to machinery behind the powerful gene-editing tool Crispr. It’s the first result from Anthropic’s newly-launched wet lab and an early test of Claude’s usefulness for science as the company prepares to go public.
Anthropic’s biolab made a discovery it’s comparing to Crispr
It took nearly 1,000 Claude agents 21 hours and 210 million tokens to uncover the ‘novel enzyme system.’
The company says Claude found the enzyme system after searching through a massive database of DNA sequences, adding that its scientists’ involvement was limited to the initial prompt and lab work.
Over 21 hours, Anthropic said nearly 950 Claude agents worked through 210 million tokens before one spotted an unusual repeating pattern in the dataset and flagged for human review. Further analysis and lab testing revealed “a previously uncharacterized enzyme system found in bacteriophages,” a type of virus that infects bacteria.
Anthropic said it is still working to understand what the enzyme system does, but said it felt it was “important to share such findings early, both to demonstrate Claude’s capabilities and to give the broader community insight into what we’re working on.”
Despite Anthropic’s comparisons to Crispr, it remains unclear whether the discovery will have any practical applications, let alone be as transformative as the gene-editing technology. The admittedly premature announcement comes as Anthropic seeks to attract more scientists to its lab and expand into areas like drug discovery.
The push comes as AI companies increasingly turn to scientific research to prove the value of their more capable models. OpenAI, meanwhile, has been barreling through increasingly advanced mathematical problems with little regard for the academic norms and traditions of the field.

articles.title: Mira el nuevo tráiler de 'You can see everything', el perturbador documental de Elizabeth Holmes: "No tengo nada que esconder"
articles.text:
El documental You can see everything (en español Puedes verlo todo) se ha convertido en uno de los estrenos más esperados del año desde el lanzamiento de su primer tráiler hace unas semanas. Ahora, la producción de Nathan Fielder centrada en la exempresaria Elizabeth Holmes acaba de sacar a la luz un nuevo avance aún más extenso. Y, una vez más, las expectativas ya están por las nubes con lo que puede ser sin duda el documental del año.
Elizabeth Holmes era una presunta mente brillante que prometía revolucionar la industria de los análisis de sangre con una sola gota. Tan innovadora era su tecnología que se convirtió en una verdadera celebridad de Silicon Valley. Incluso se la llegó a comparar con Steve Jobs. Pero que la realidad es que todo era mentira, estafó a sus inversores y acabó en prisión.
Y justo un mes antes de que Holmes entrara a la cárcel, ella misma contactó con Nathan Fielder para grabar una suerte de documental. "Creo que es el momento de capturar esta historia antes de que ya no esté", llega a confesar ella en el nuevo tráiler de You can see everything. "¿No te preocupa que yo esté aquí constantemente?", le pregunta él. "No, creo que no", responde ella. "¿Y qué pasa si veo algo que dé mala imagen de ti?", insiste él, ante la mirada penetrante de la fundadora de Theranos.
Mira el tráiler de You can see everything
Aunque fue Elizabeth Holmes quien contactó con Nathan Fielder para hacer un breve documental de un mes, el cineasta quedó tan cautivado por su perturbadora personalidad que decidió seguir grabando y visitándola dentro de la prisión. Así nació lo que ahora será You can see everything, una producción que se estrena en Estados Unidos en apenas unas pocas semanas, el 16 de octubre. En España y Latinoamérica todavía no cuenta con fecha de estreno.
Lo que es evidente es que, antes de You can see everything, la obsesión de Nathan Fielder por jugar con realidad y ficción ya había dado sus frutos. El actor y director también es responsable de títulos tremendamente aclamados y difíciles de describir como las series Nathan For You, The Curse o, sobre todo, Los ensayos. Ahora, promete volver a impactar con un documental inédito sobre una de las personalidades más reconocibles de Estados Unidos en el siglo XXI.

articles.title: Eight Sleep's new Pod 6 comes in smaller and solo sizes, starting at $1,999 | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Sleep tech company Eight Sleep on Wednesday launched its new Pod 6 device in a smaller size than previous editions to fit more bed frames, along with solo sizes for one-person use. The company said that the device can be used to adjust the temperature on either side 20% faster than the previous-generation gadget.
Because the new pod has a 50% smaller footprint, it can fit most bed frames. The company claims the device has 9x more sensors, enabling it to understand granular temperature controls for each user even if they are sleeping close together. Plus, it can ignore data from a pet or a kid sleeping on the bed with two users.
The Pod 6 is available starting today in over 37 countries, starting at $1,999 for solo sizes and $2,699 for standard sizes. Solo sizes can fit a twin bed and one side of queen, king, and California King beds. Standard sizes will be available in queen, king, and California King. Plus, it can work with existing add-ons like a blanket, pillow cover, and base.
Beyond new sleep products, the company is pursuing Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval to transition its Eight Sleep Pod into a regulated medical device for sleep apnea in the U.S.
Earlier this year, the company raised $50 million from Tether at a $1.5 billion valuation. Eight Sleep also took steps to expand its international footprint by launching its product in China, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Singapore in the last year, with China becoming one of the fastest-growing regions.
The company’s CEO Matteo Franceschetti told TechCrunch that international markets contribute over 30% of revenue. He mentioned that the sleep tech company plans to expand into other regions of Asia and Latin America. Franceschetti noted that the company is keeping a keen eye on the component crunch in the electronics sector, but didn’t say whether it will impact pricing.
“We definitely see the market changing a little bit because AI companies are requesting a lot of different components. We are adjusting our supply chain [to counter that]. It’s definitely something that we need to watch out for, particularly as our devices become more and more, I would say, compute-heavy and intelligent to be able to provide AI features to our users,” he said.

articles.title: Google will pay off its new €403M GDPR fine in just 55 hours, warns Proton
articles.text:
Google will pay off its new €403M GDPR fine in just 55 hours, warns Proton
Ireland's Data Protection Commission has slapped Google with the largest ever fine for unlawfully processing users' location data between 2018 and 2020
- Google hit with €403M for the unlawful processing of user location data
- Proton calculates Alphabet can cover the penalty in just about two days
- Multi-million fines are failing to deter Big Tech repeating GDPR violations
The news that Ireland's Data Protection Commission (DPC) fined Google €403 million (around $462 million) for the unlawful processing of users' location data may sound like a monumental victory for consumer privacy. Yet, industry experts are already warning that the fine is simply too small to force a change in corporate behavior.
According to the privacy firm Proton, Google's parent company, Alphabet, will be able to brush off the historic penalty in less time than it takes to enjoy a long weekend.
"Google will barely notice this fine," noted Jurgita Miseviciute, Head of Public Policy at Proton. "When one of the biggest weapons in the EU's arsenal only costs the offender two days of revenue, it's not a deterrence."
For everyday internet users looking to protect their digital footprint with the best VPN or secure browser, this latest ruling serves as a stark reminder of how profitable your personal data remains.
Proton VPN – best for privacy 
Based in Switzerland, this privacy-first VPN offers good speeds, advanced anti-censorship features, and a server network that spans 145 countries around the world — including across Africa and Asia, where other providers tend to struggle. While its free VPN plan is handy, it comes with limitations. The good news is that upgrading to a premium subscription will cost you only the equivalent of $2.99 per month.
A multi-million euro 'slap on the wrist'
Following a lengthy inquiry, the DPC announced the enforcement action against Google over controversial location data practices that occurred between 2018 and 2020. It represents one of the largest GDPR penalties the search giant has ever faced.
However, for a company the size of Alphabet, the impact is mathematically minuscule. Based on Alphabet’s own reported 2025 free cash flow of $73.3 billion, which breaks down to roughly $200 million a day, Proton notes that Google's cash flow alone could cover the fine in about two days and seven hours.
To put that into perspective, that is roughly 55 hours, or 199,000 seconds of standard revenue generation.
NEW: Leave No Trace — A weekly newsletter on digital privacy and online surveillance.
Leave No Trace investigates the companies and governments putting our digital freedom at risk — and the people fighting back.
📩 Subscribe now to get every edition delivered to your inbox every Friday, launching this September.
The illusion of deterrence
The €403 million fine is not an isolated incident. In 2025 alone, Google picked up five separate fines totaling nearly $4.24 billion. Thanks to its massive financial reserves, the company's free cash flow could replace that entire sum in roughly three weeks, a trend that echoes broader warnings that Big Tech could need only one month to pay off over $7 billion in collective 2025 fines.
This mirrors an equally dismal pattern from the previous year, when the industry needed less than three weeks to pay off over $8 billion in 2024 penalties.
This recurring pattern has left privacy advocates frustrated by the limitations of the European Union's current regulatory framework.
Miseviciute from Proton emphasized that the lack of financial sting makes these penalties a mere cost of doing business rather than a mechanism for actual reform.
"Time and time again fines makes [sic] headlines without changing Big Tech's behaviour at all," she added. "If regulators are serious about compliance, the penalties have to actually bite."
For consumers, this means the responsibility for data security largely remains in their own hands. Location data is uniquely sensitive, capable of revealing everything from your home address to your daily routines and medical visits.
Until regulators find a way to issue penalties that genuinely threaten a tech giant's bottom line, companies will continue to calculate that the astronomical profits of aggressive data harvesting far outweigh the minor risks of a regulatory fine.

With over two decades of experience as a reporter and editor, he specializes in making complex topics like cybersecurity, VPNs, and enterprise software accessible and engaging.

articles.title: Germany's SPRIND and the Netherlands' NADI launch €40 million challenge to fast-track European AI chip design | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Germany’s Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation (SPRIND) and its Dutch counterpart, the National Agency for Disruptive Innovation (NADI), have launched a joint €40 million programme to fund radical innovations in pan-European chip design.
Announced today, the AI-Native Chip Design Challenge marks the first joint-funding initiative between SPRIND and NADI. It aims to cut chip development timelines from years to weeks and strengthen Europe’s sovereign AI capabilities.
“The launch of NADI’s first programme is a huge statement of Europe’s intent to combine two of the continent’s greatest strengths: collaboration and innovation… We expect to see more nations commit to backing pan-European, radical breakthroughs. The need is great, and the model works,” said Jano Costard, Head of Challenges, SPRIND.
The AI-Native Chip Design Challenge will run across two stages over 20 months. Stage 1, from November to July 2027, will select seven teams, each receiving €2.6 million. Stage 2 will run for a further year, shortlisting three teams to receive €7 million each. Beyond capital, participating teams will get technical and commercial coaching to help bring their chip designs to market. Further financing details and dates for Stage 1 are still to be confirmed.
The Challenge seeks to scale the use of AI-driven methods in chip design, leaning on AI models now capable of reaching technical conclusions and reinforcement-learning agents able to independently tackle complex optimisation problems, with the eventual goal of AI systems handling chip design autonomously. The programme also aims to produce production-ready chip designs for high-performance AI inference and training, improving energy efficiency, scalability, and inference costs.
NADI was formally announced on 15 September 2026, when Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Heleen Herbert unveiled the agency on Prinsjesdag, the country’s annual Budget Day. It is built on the ARPA model already used by SPRIND from 2019 and by the UK’s ARIA from 2022. NADI is designed to run challenge-style programmes around specific technological problems facing the Netherlands and Europe, with the government allocating €500 million and acting as an early customer to help innovations reach the market faster.
At the time of the announcement, the minister asked entrepreneur and Cradle founder Jelle Prins to build out the organisation alongside DeepTech investor Beau-Anne Chilla. Both previously sat on the Ministry of Economic Affairs’ NADI expert panel.
The formation of NADI follows an open letter from universities, university medical centres, investors, and major companies, including Philips and NXP, with further support from Peter Wennink, former chief executive of ASML. The widely circulated Wennink Report, which called for technology and innovation investment, recommended that the Dutch government commit €1.5 to 2 billion to NADI’s deployment budget.
“NADI’s mission is to catalyse breakthrough innovation in areas of significant societal and economic importance. We are excited to run our first Challenge together with SPRIND, on a topic that is strategically relevant for the Netherlands and Europe. SPRIND has been advising the Dutch government on how to set up NADI, and this collaboration is the next opportunity for us to learn from their experience,” said Jelle Prins, co-founder of NADI.
SPRIND, whose Challenges model has deployed more than €100 million across Europe this year, has supported NADI’s formation. Earlier this year, SPRIND launched its first joint Challenge with Sweden’s Vinnova; it also collaborates with the US ARPAs and the National Science Foundation.
Europe currently relies on the US and China for semiconductor supply, a dependency exposed by this year’s energy-price pressures and supply-chain disruption. Chip design remains among the costliest and most technically demanding engineering fields, and Europe’s nascent AI-driven design market is seen as a structural bottleneck holding back the region’s wider AI ambitions.
The Challenge, which draws on the Netherlands’ €33.6 billion semiconductor sector, anchored by ASML, alongside Germany’s DeepTech and industrial manufacturing base, led by firms such as Siemens and Bosch, is seen as the first step to create technological sovereignty.

articles.title: Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India
articles.text:
Smart glasses are already causing havoc in India
And the chances of a crackdown are slim, as the authorities spy opportunities for surveillance.
Shubnam was packing boxes for a move into a new home when their friend sent them an Instagram video. The footage had only been up for a few hours, but it was days old, recorded at a Delhi protest this spring against a bill that would have narrowed the legal recognition for transgender people in India.
There, a content creator known for rage-bait videos had approached Shubnam, a 38-year-old transfeminine graphic designer and educator. Shubnam, who uses a single chosen name, was dressed in a green sari with a shaved head, and the creator asked why they were wearing “female clothing.” Shubnam told him to back off. Only when the video arrived did they realize he had recorded the exchange on Meta smart glasses, styled to look like ordinary Wayfarers.
Edited into a mocking reel, the footage drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse, reaction videos, and AI-generated memes. It spread from Instagram to X and YouTube. Copies remain online today.
For Shubnam, the video has caused huge harm. “All it took was one unconsented video to rewind two decades of progress that I made all on my own,” they told MIT Technology Review. “For a moment, it felt like this entire adult life I had lived was just a long lucid dream, and I was going to wake up as that clueless queer child again.” They haven’t worn a sari outside their neighborhood since.
Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream. And they say privacy problems are becoming especially acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive.
Cases of cyberstalking, sextortion, deepfakes, and other forms of online abuse are growing in the country. And the chances of a crackdown on technologies such as smart glasses are slim, given that Indian law enforcement authorities are themselves increasingly adopting AI-powered surveillance tools, including facial recognition systems and their own AI-enabled smart glasses.
An unequal burden
Smart glasses are among the fastest-growing devices in India’s wearables market, according to the International Data Corporation, a research firm. And Reliance Jio, one of the country’s largest telecommunications companies, says that later this year it’s set to launch a sub-$105 rival to Meta’s glasses, the latest model of which have a $420 price tag in India.
The core privacy issue is that these cameras don’t look like cameras, so targets may not notice they’re being recorded. Yet Meta rejects the idea that it’s responsible for protecting people from intrusions, says Janusz Świerczyński, an Oxford Saïd Business School researcher who studies privacy and emerging technology.
“More and more, the expectation is being placed on bystanders to look out for themselves,” he says. That means it’s up to them to spot a small LED in the glasses frames that activates when recording is in progress. Meta also relies on wearers to behave responsibly, says Świerczyński. Reliance Jio did not respond to our request for comment on privacy issues related to its upcoming glasses.
Creators have already demonstrated ways to circumvent the recording light on Meta’s glasses. Tutorials show users how to cover or otherwise obscure the LED while continuing to record. Back in March, Wired documented a market for “stealth mode” modifications that physically disable the light or remove it entirely.
All that makes covert recording easier, and the risks are not borne equally. Świerczyński says women and other marginalized groups face greater harm when inconspicuous devices capture and circulate footage without consent—as happened to Shubnam.
The bigger problem, however, is that in India smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also being adopted as a tool of police surveillance.
In June, when thousands of young demonstrators gathered to protest problems with the country’s education system, Delhi police used Meta smart glasses to record them. In fact, a petition filed by former Jawaharlal Nehru University Students’ Union president Aishe Ghosh before the Delhi High Court alleged that police had filmed protesters continuously for weeks, including while they were eating and resting. It also alleged that the police had threatened to send footage of student demonstrators to their parents and colleges.
In July, India’s solicitor general dismissed the case in court as “luxury litigation.” Instead of investigating the students’ complaints, police turned on the students themselves, opening 10 criminal investigations for offenses including rioting, assault on public servants, and damage to public property. Some of the protesters, who spoke to MIT Technology Review on condition of anonymity, say they never saw the LED on the Meta AI glasses police wore during the demonstrations.
Filming without consent
Meta maintains that its safeguard works. The company told MIT Technology Review, “Every pair has a capture LED that blinks when you take a photo or video that you can save or share; it can’t be turned off, and if someone covers or damages the LED, the camera is disabled.” The company also says users are responsible for complying with the law and respecting people’s privacy.
That approach is risky, especially in India, where norms around filming and consent are still highly disputed and digital literacy is still uneven, says Sameer Parmar, a counselor at Meri Trustline, a safety partner working with Meta and YouTube to support people harmed by online content.
“The hardware is improving, but the country’s weak understanding of consent gives an invisible camera far more room to cause harm,” he says. Simply being in a public place is often treated as implicit consent to be photographed or filmed. He says the help line has been seeing an uptick in cases involving covert recording and nonconsensual footage.
“Violations of this access have increased significantly and are expected to rise further in India,” he says. People are recorded in medical settings, during private encounters, and in public spaces. Those with less power to object are particularly vulnerable, he adds.
“It’s either trolling or it’s playing pranks on them and then recording them” he says. Abusers “do target people who are a little more unaware or susceptible to how this technology-facilitated harm works.”
The law in India has not caught up with this new kind of harm, says Apar Gupta, a lawyer and founder-director of the Internet Freedom Foundation. “India’s laws against voyeurism and the sharing of intimate images were designed largely around more recognizable forms of abuse,” he says, citing offenses such as secretly filming someone undressing, using a toilet, or engaged in a sexual act. “[The laws] offer limited protection when someone is secretly filmed in an ordinary public setting and the footage is then used to humiliate them,” he says.
Social media platforms’ rules do offer another route to removing harmful content filmed with smart glasses, but it’s not an immediate remedy. “Under India’s current rules, platforms can have up to 36 hours to act on certain complaints—a window that can be long enough for a video to be downloaded, copied, and circulated elsewhere,” he says.
The problem of filming without consent seems set to grow. According to the Financial Times, some internal prototypes of new Meta glasses include AI features that continuously photograph and listen to the wearer’s surroundings, enabling the glasses to later recall what they saw or heard. These functions wouldn’t activate the external recording indicator, making it impossible for bystanders to know when information about them is being collected.
Meta told us it intends to keep the LED for active capture, such as taking photos or recording video, but not for AI features that interpret the wearer’s surroundings. Its argument is that a constantly blinking light could eventually become so commonplace that people stop noticing it.
But that logic risks putting society in a perpetual game of catch-up, says Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law at Boston University. “Tech companies have an incredible ability to push these tools out faster than society can meaningfully acclimate to the threat,” he says. “By the time society catches up, there’s already a degree of normalization.”
For Shubnam, the danger is not just that people may become accustomed to being recorded. It is that they will become accustomed to seeing versions of themselves that they never chose to put out into the world.
“Being comprehended along the lines of a narrative that I didn’t compose or consent to—that imposed recognition makes you feel like you’re powerless in how people know you,” they say.

articles.title: Microsoft et la police britannique démantèlent EvilTokens, le service de phishing lié à 12 000 comptes piratés
articles.text:
La police londonienne a arrêté deux hommes de 32 et 38 ans, soupçonnés d'administrer EvilTokens, pendant que Microsoft saisissait 50 sites web liés à ce service d'hameçonnage par abonnement. Depuis février, ses clients ont compromis plus de 12 000 boîtes mail Microsoft 365 sans jamais voler de mot de passe.
On vous parlait ce printemps de l'essor des kits de phishing par code d'appareil vendus clés en main sur Telegram. Ces attaques avaient multipliées par 37,5 selon les chercheurs de Push Security, seulement en quelques semaines, et EvilTokens était l'une des plateformes les plus utilisées, d'après Microsoft.
Les pirates détournent une méthode de connexion prévue par Microsoft pour les téléviseurs connectés et les autres appareils sans clavier. L'utilisateur lit un code court sur l'écran de l'appareil, puis le saisit depuis un ordinateur ou un smartphone pour l'autoriser. Avec EvilTokens, l'attaquant génère ce code avant de l'envoyer à sa cible. En le saisissant sur la véritable page microsoft.com/devicelogin, la victime autorise la session du pirate, double authentification comprise, le tout à son insu.
Le kit EvilTokens vendu 1 500 dollars sur Telegram
Pour les équipes de Microsoft Threat Intelligence, Storm-2992 est le groupe à l'origine d'EvilTokens, sans lien connu avec les grands réseaux cybercriminels. Ses membres vendaient le kit 1 500 dollars sur leurs chaînes Telegram, puis 500 dollars par mois pour garder l'accès au panneau de contrôle, et facturaient à part plusieurs modules complémentaires, dont un outil de redirection antibot. Une fois connecté, l'abonné choisissait l'un des 44 thèmes de leurres proposés, de la fausse facture à l'appel d'offres, et pouvait confier la rédaction de l'e-mail à un assistant d'intelligence artificielle, avec un message adapté au poste du destinataire.
Après l'intrusion, l'abonné conservait un accès complet à la boîte mail de la victime, avec un renouvellement automatique des jetons et des alertes par mots-clés reçues sur Telegram. Dans notre article de juillet consacré à EvilTokens, vous pouviez lire qu'un jeton d'actualisation volé est valable environ 90 jours. Les pirates utilisaient aussi l'IA de la plateforme pour repérer, au sein des comptes compromis, les salariés habilités à valider des paiements, puis fouiller leurs échanges à la recherche de virements et de factures en attente. « L'IA n'aidait pas simplement les attaquants à écrire des messages plus convaincants. Elle les aidait à décider qui cibler », a expliqué Steven Masada, conseiller juridique adjoint de la Digital Crimes Unit de Microsoft, cité par CyberScoop.
Tanmay Ganacharya est vice-président de la recherche en sécurité chez Microsoft. Il a indiqué à The Register que ses équipes observaient chaque jour entre 10 et 15 nouvelles campagnes depuis le 15 mars. Au total, plus de 12 000 boîtes mail ont été compromises dans plus de 10 000 organisations, en France, aux États-Unis, au Canada, au Royaume-Uni, en Australie et en Inde. Pour les opérateurs d'EvilTokens, l'affaire était rentable. Ils ont encaissé environ 1,1 million de dollars en cryptomonnaies grâce à plus de 1 000 dépôts venus de 700 adresses, d'après les données de Coinbase publiées par CyberScoop.
Deux administrateurs présumés d'EvilTokens arrêtés à Londres
En août, Microsoft a transmis ses conclusions à la police métropolitaine de Londres. Le 18 septembre, les policiers ont perquisitionné deux adresses à Canary Wharf et à Nine Elms, où ils ont arrêté deux hommes de 32 et 38 ans, soupçonnés de fabrication d'articles destinés à la fraude et de blanchiment d'argent. Tous deux sont libres sous caution pendant la suite de l'enquête, et Microsoft n'a pas dévoilé leur identité. « La Met est déterminée à demander des comptes aux personnes qui facilitent des activités criminelles en pensant passer inaperçues. Nous vous trouverons et nous agirons », a prévenu Serena D'Adamo, inspectrice de la police métropolitaine. Un porte-parole de Microsoft a ajouté que d'autres personnes avaient probablement soutenu le service.
Trois jours avant ces arrestations, un tribunal fédéral de Virginie avait autorisé Microsoft et Health-ISAC à saisir l'infrastructure du service. Cette organisation mutualise les alertes de cybersécurité des établissements de santé. Avec Cloudflare, Coinbase, OpenAI ou encore TRM Labs, les deux organisations ont mis hors ligne 50 sites web et désactivé plus de 150 domaines. Microsoft en est à sa 40e action de ce genre validée par un tribunal.
Dans les entreprises, Microsoft conseille de bloquer la connexion par code d'appareil au moyen des stratégies d'accès conditionnel d'Entra ID, sauf pour les rares équipements incompatibles avec une autre méthode. Quand un administrateur révoque les sessions d'un compte compromis, les jetons d'accès sont encore valides jusqu'à une heure, si bien que l'éditeur recommande de désactiver temporairement le compte. Au printemps, Push Security recensait d'ailleurs plus de dix kits concurrents. « L'infrastructure d'EvilTokens a été démantelée, mais le modèle qu'elle a démontré ne disparaîtra pas avec elle », a averti Steven Masada.

articles.title: Smarter Buildings, Safer Occupants: Intelligence Meets Privacy - EE Times
articles.text:
Personal safety and security allow no compromise. From access control and video surveillance to smoke and fire alarms, HVAC, and lighting, modern building automation systems are designed to optimize energy efficiency while safeguarding the health, safety, and security of occupants.
In this Special Report, we explore how ambient light harvesting is expanding into buildings and how advanced sensors and AI-driven IoT solutions enable real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and faster emergency response—without compromising individual privacy.
What happens when sensors become ubiquitous? Can buildings harvest enough ambient energy to power their own sensors? Can buildings use light not just to illuminate spaces but also to power IoT devices, day and night? How can cameras improve safety without identifying individuals? Where should the intelligence reside: at the edge or in the cloud? How can increasingly connected building systems integrate without creating new security risks?
To answer these questions, this Special Report draws on interviews with companies such as Axis Communications, e-peas, Infineon Technologies, and Pimloc, as well as discussions with professors from the University of North Carolina at Charlotte, the Laboratory for Future Interdisciplinary Research of Science and Technology at the Institute of Science Tokyo, and the Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar. It also features contributions from Wireless Logic and Insight SiP.
Ambient IoT: From Battery-Free Promise to Mass-Market Reality
By Rebecca Pool
Surging investment, maturing tech, and emerging standards are pushing ambient IoT toward mainstream deployment.
Digital Keys and Radio Technology in Smart Buildings
By Nick Wood, Insight SiP
The direction of travel seems clear enough: Digital keys are likely to replace physical ones entirely over time.
How Much Impact Will AI Have on IoT Software Engineering?
By Steve Bennett, Wireless Logic
In theory, AI is a surefire way to raise productivity in software engineering, but the reality may not be quite so cut-and-dried.
LEDs Push Wireless Power Further
By Rebecca Pool
An LED alternative to laser wireless power transfer from the Institute of Science Tokyo uses adaptive optics and AI beam steering to charge indoor IoT devices 5 meters away.
Smarter Cameras Need More Than Edge AI to Protect Privacy
By Pat Brans
Axis Communications and Pimloc show how masking, encryption, anonymization, and
governance can protect privacy without destroying useful evidence.
The Security AI That Learns the Language of Movement
By Pat Brans
UNC Charlotte researchers use edge AI to learn normal motion, predict what comes next, and flag anomalies for human review.
India Hardens Its Cyber Defenses
By Rebecca Pool
As cyberthreats target critical infrastructure and India’s online population tops 1 billion, digital resilience is now a national security priority.

articles.title: Android 17 : Google prépare le retour d'une option géniale disparue depuis des années
articles.text:
Mettre un code PIN complexe pour sécuriser son smartphone est une bonne idée, à condition de ne pas l’oublier. Jusqu’à présent, la seule issue pour retrouver l’usage de son mobile consistait à effacer toutes ses données locales non sauvegardées. Mais une nouvelle option plus simple pourrait réapparaître, comme le révèle le code de la version QPR2 Beta 5 d’Android 17.
Un retour en arrière salvateur ?
La fonction en question s’appelle « Déverrouiller avec le Compte Google » et permet comme son nom l’indique de débloquer un appareil récalcitrant. Une telle option existait déjà sous Android 4.4 KitKat et les versions antérieures, avant d’être supprimée par l’entreprise avec l’arrivée d’Android 5.0. Google avait ensuite introduit la protection contre la réinitialisation d’usine pour empêcher les voleurs de réutiliser un téléphone volé après un effacement forcé en mode Récupération.
La fonction a été dénichée par nos confrères d’Android Authority dans une section dédiée au verrouillage de l’appareil (là où l’on paramètre habituellement ses codes et ses empreintes digitales). La description de l’option est assez explicite :
« Si vous oubliez votre PIN ou votre mot de passe, déverrouillez votre appareil en utilisant votre compte Google associé ».
Actuellement inactive dans cette bêta, la nouveauté s’adresse avant tout à ceux qui redoutent la perte définitive de leurs photos et fichiers locaux sans pour autant avoir commis une erreur de sécurité majeure.
Une option facultative
Cette future fonctionnalité est évidemment plus commode pour le grand public qui va pouvoir récupérer son compte facilement, mais on ne peut évidemment pas totalement écarter le risque qu’une personne malintentionnée mette la main sur le téléphone tout en réussissant à deviner ou obtenir le mot de passe du compte Google associé. Il pourrait ainsi mettre la main sur les données personnelles qui sont présentes sur l’appareil.
À lire : Android 17 réduit drastiquement le nombre de tentatives pour rentrer votre mot de passe
Les utilisateurs très attachés à la sécurité de leurs données personnelles pourront donc choisir de désactiver ou d’ignorer cette option s’ils estiment que le risque d’oublier leur code secret est infime, acceptant par avance le principe d’un effacement total de leurs données en cas de pépin. Reste à savoir si Google déploiera officiellement cette option dans une future mise stable d’Android, les indices découverts dans le code d’une bêta ne garantissant jamais une intégration définitive dans la version publique.

articles.title: F5 patches BIG-IP APM zero-day flaw exploited in RCE attacks
articles.text:
F5 has released security updates to address a critical BIG-IP APM zero-day vulnerability being exploited in remote code execution attacks.
BIG-IP APM (short for Access Policy Manager) is the company's centralized access management proxy solution that helps admins secure access to their organizations' networks, applications, cloud, and application programming interfaces (APIs).
Tracked as CVE-2026-94127, the flaw affects instances configured as an OAuth Authorization Server when a BIG-IP APM access policy and an OAuth profile are configured on a virtual server.
"We have learned that this vulnerability has been exploited," F5 warned in a security advisory published on Tuesday. "Deployments using APM strictly as an OAuth Client / Resource Server (without OAuth authorization server profiles configured) are not affected by this vulnerability."
The company advised customers to review systems for indicators of compromise if they detect a combination of multiple OAuth authentication failures and suspicious commands, shortly followed by a TMM SIGABRT.
F5 also shared mitigation measures for admins who can't immediately install the security updates, which require applying an iRule (available from F5 Support) to the affected BIG-IP APM virtual server.
Internet threat monitoring non-profit Shadowserver currently tracks over 14,700 IP addresses with BIG-IP APM fingerprints. However, there is no information on how many have already been patched or are honeypots.
On Tuesday, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) also added CVE-2026-94127 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and ordered U.S. federal agencies to secure their networks against this flaw by Friday.
"These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise," the cybersecurity agency warned.
Cybercrime and state-backed threat groups have often exploited F5 vulnerabilities in recent years. For instance, attackers have targeted security flaws in F5 products to breach corporate networks, hijack devices, map internal servers, deploy data-wiping malware, and steal sensitive documents.
F5 also disclosed in October 2025 that state-sponsored hackers breached its systems in August 2025 and stole undisclosed BIG-IP security source code and vulnerabilities.
Since November 2021, CISA has flagged eight actively exploited F5 vulnerabilities, four of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.
F5 is a Fortune 500 company that provides cybersecurity, application delivery networking (ADN), and other services to more than 23,000 customers worldwide, including 48 of the Fortune 50 companies and 80% of the Fortune Global 500.
Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.

articles.title: DREO lance ses chauffages d'appoint connectés et promet jusqu'à 40 % d'économies d'énergie
articles.text:
Vous connaissez peut-être DREO pour ses ventilateurs et climatiseurs connectés, arrivés en France pile pendant les canicules de l’été. La marque change de saison et attaque le chauffage, un virage qu’elle avait déjà dévoilé début septembre à l’IFA de Berlin. Ce 23 septembre 2026 elle lance tout d’un coup : deux radiateurs d’appoint et un purificateur d’air.
Le modèle vedette, c’est le Chauffage 360° 720S, vendu 119,99 euros. Son argument : une technologie maison baptisée AutoShift 360°, qui oriente la chaleur soit vers vous en mode Ciblé, soit dans toute la pièce en mode 360°, pour des surfaces de 15 à 25 m². Une résistance céramique chauffe en quelques secondes, à 25 décibels annoncés, avec un éclairage d’ambiance qui vire de couleur selon la chauffe.
Le Convecteur 711S, lui, coûte plus cher : 149,99 euros. Il chauffe par convection naturelle, sans ventilateur, ce qui le rend totalement silencieux (0 décibel selon DREO). Son format mural ultra-fin en verre trempé libère le sol et vise les petites pièces où l’on cherche une chaleur stable, avec une résistance de 2000 watts.
Reste le Purificateur d’air 530S, à 139,99 euros, un peu à part dans cette gamme hiver. Il annonce une filtration en trois étapes qui retient 99,97 % des particules jusqu’à 0,3 micron en mode Sommeil, avec un capteur PM2.5 qui ajuste la vitesse tout seul et une application pour suivre la qualité de l’air.
Les 40 % d’économies, qu’est-ce que ça vaut vraiment ?
Les deux chauffages partagent un mode ECO que DREO crédite de « jusqu’à 40 % » d’économies d’énergie. Le « jusqu’à » pose question, car la marque ne dit pas par rapport à quel usage. Surtout, tous les chauffages électriques à résistance ont le même rendement : 100 %. Un radiateur ne fabrique pas de chaleur miracle, il transforme l’électricité en chaleur. L’économie vient donc du mode ECO, qui chauffe moins fort ou cible mieux la zone à réchauffer.
Pour qui, alors ? Un studio, une chambre où l’on veut du silence, un bureau de télétravail : ces DREO y trouvent leur place, surtout le convecteur 711S et son fonctionnement à 0 décibel. Pour chauffer tout un logement à longueur de journée, mieux vaut regarder du côté d’un chauffage central. Les trois produits sont en vente dès maintenant sur le site de DREO, sur Amazon et chez les revendeurs agréés.

articles.title: Adobe Patches Critical Flaws in Connect, AEM Forms
articles.text:
Adobe on Tuesday rolled out patches for 36 vulnerabilities across its products, including critical-severity flaws in Connect and Experience Manager (AEM) Forms.
The Adobe Connect update resolves nine security defects, including six critical issues that could be exploited for arbitrary code execution and privilege escalation.
Tracked as CVE-2026-75682, CVE-2026-75684, CVE-2026-75686, CVE-2026-75689, CVE-2026-75697, and CVE-2026-75698, they are described as SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS), and improper input validation flaws.
The update also fixes high-severity path traversal, improper certificate validation, and XSS weaknesses that could lead to arbitrary file system read, security feature bypass, and arbitrary code execution.
Adobe patched six vulnerabilities in AEM Forms, including three critical-severity flaws leading to code execution and privilege escalation.
Described as incorrect authorization, improper input validation, and server-side request forgery (SSRF), the critical issues are tracked as CVE-2026-75745, CVE-2026-81995, and CVE-2026-82000.
The AEM Forms patches also fix three high-severity SSRF, XSS, and cross-site request forgery (CSRF) bugs leading to privilege escalation, code execution, and security feature bypass.
Both security updates have a priority 2 rating, meaning that users should apply them within the next 30 days.
On Tuesday, Adobe also announced fixes for multiple high- and medium-severity vulnerabilities in InDesign, Content Credentials SDK, Bridge, Substance 3D Modeler, and Premiere Pro.
Successful exploitation of these security defects could lead to application denial-of-service (DoS), security feature bypass, arbitrary code execution, and memory exposure.
Adobe says it is not aware of any of these security flaws being exploited in the wild. Additional information is available on the company’s security bulletins page.

articles.title: Multi-Agent AI Systems Must Work Like An Orchestra Without A Conductor
articles.text:
A mixture of expert agentic AI systems can focus on their tasks with or without a commanding general, but challenges remain in drawing boundaries between human and AI effort.
Key Takeaways:
Experts At The Table: Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss recent developments and challenges when using agentic AI for chip design, with Matt Graham, senior group director of verification software product management at Cadence; Harrison Balistreri, head of business development and strategic partnerships at ChipAgents; Alexander Petr, senior director and portfolio manager at Keysight EDA; Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at Siemens EDA; and Anand Thiruvengadam, executive director and head of AI product management at Synopsys. This roundtable was held behind closed doors at the recent Design Automation Conference. What follows are excerpts of that discussion. This is the third part of a three-part series. Part one is here. Part two is here.
L-R: Synopsys’ Thiruvengadam; Keysight’s Petr; Cadence’s Graham; ChipAgents’ Balistreri; and Siemens’ Balasubramanian.
SE: Many agentic flows involve a mixture of experts (MoE) or a hierarchy of multi-agents with some type of leader at the top. What developments are you seeing there? Is it a top-down, military-style organization with various security and access clearances, or more of a horizontal team?
Graham: It is becoming much flatter than an army. If you’d asked me a year ago, I might have said, yes, it is a big hierarchy of agents. There will be mini agents, sub agents, and low agents. There will be generals and lieutenants and whatever else, all the way up. But AI in general, not just EDA, we are migrating much more toward a flat set of skills, or capabilities, or features, or knowledge, or whatever the word is you want to use to describe it. Everything is overloaded with terms. What we’re seeing becomes a much more dynamic, task-based organization of skills into almost dynamic agents. There is one general, if you like, or commander.
Balasubramanian: Orchestrator.
Graham: Right. And everything else below tends to be much flatter. I can pick and choose quickly to assemble my troops, but it’s much less like an army with a mechanized division and an airborne division, or something else. We have troops. Those troops have skills, and we assemble the right troops for the task dynamically, because we’re not bound, as armies are, by logistical and physical reality.
Petr: You’re better off comparing it to an orchestra. You have one conductor, and you have groups who play certain instruments. They can play individually, or they can play together. They can also play synchronously or asynchronously to achieve certain tunes and then play together.
Balasubramanian: That’s very important. Even if it’s flat, the key thing is that everyone knows their part, and they also know how they connect to everyone else. Everyone knows the end goal. Nothing is siloed. They all play by the same tune. If you look at a symphony orchestra, everyone knows everyone else. They can read the notes. They know what to do, what not to do, how to do it.
Petr: There are borders, guardrails. They all ground it.
Balasubramanian: The term I see quite a bit is headless agents. There’s no concept of having a big master agent doing everything else. We call it a headless way of working, and it’s been quite popular on the software side. It’s coming here, and what I see going forward is customers are interacting with tools. They won’t even know what the tool is. From our side, we are going to build agentic capabilities coming out of the physical engines, or deterministic engines around those engines, and that’s going to be an agent on its own. It can talk to other agents. It can understand different formats and where it sits. It can talk to understand design. Designers can interact with it, make it do work. That’s where the future is going.
Thiruvengadam: What Matt said is very interesting. We are essentially making the point that you should be thinking about digital organization—human organization, human hierarchy, digital hierarchy, roughly speaking —which is correct. But also, the fluidity of that is very important. It won’t be a rigid, hard structure. Ebb and flow will happen. It can change, depending on the complexity of the commands. The fluidity is very important. You will have a layer that orchestrates and calls upon ‘resources’ as needed to execute. This is very important. At some point in the future, it might graduate to something where it’s maybe autonomous. That is about abstraction again. We are talking about taking layer after layer of abstraction away, one by one, but we’re not there yet.
Balistreri: We have products where agents propose hypotheses and do tournament-style ranking. We have a judging agent, but there’s a lot of nuance in this idea of agents, where you could throw many agents at the problem. But if they all come up with similar hypotheses for the problem, it doesn’t matter how many agents you deploy or how good your judging agent is. It has a lot to do with how you manage context, and it comes back to local versus global context. It doesn’t matter how you deploy agents if they all have the same local context. To get the benefit of deploying agents at scale, you need to manage which hypotheses each agent generates and where that context comes from. To do that, you also can’t have point agents. You can’t do point acceleration around one tool. Agents become powerful when they can deliver the full flow. The full flow requires encoding in your agent loops how to view some of this context and how to manage that, so that you get the benefit of many parallel agents instead of them just trying to converge on the same thing.
Graham: There are two sides to that, and I agree for the most part. But I’ll draw a parallel to how synthesis changed electronic design. The vast majority of gates built now are synthesized gates. The agent writes RTL. Then, RTL gets synthesized. But there is still a certain percentage, depending on the application, that must be either hand-synthesized or laid out by hand. There will still be significant opportunity to accelerate the tools. I wouldn’t call it a point agent necessarily. But in agentifying the tool for a specific task, a smaller percentage will still need to be hand-coded, in the same way that we still hand-assemble some instructions for a PC or for any compute platform. Expecting 100% autonomy is setting too high a bar that I don’t know we can achieve. I don’t think it’s realistic or even worthwhile. Setting it at 99-point-some-odd-nines still leaves a huge amount of work to be done, and accelerating the tools themselves is still important, but I agree that it’s not the bulk of the time.
Balistreri: This might be an unpopular opinion in this room, but we can talk about accelerating existing tools, or we can talk about new tools entirely. When we talk to our customers, one of the biggest bottlenecks in taping out their chips is that they don’t have enough on-premises compute to run existing EDA tools. Can you rearchitect tools to be optimized for agent use, speed up runtime, and run more tools in parallel? Then there’s the other question of, ‘Do the models subsume it?’ In some of the complex tasks that are still hand-placed, there is an opportunity for models to take that on and solve extremely complex problems that humans just couldn’t hold in their heads. Think about all those tables you had to look at on the wall. Back in the day, you were laying sheets across a giant table to look at the resistance and capacitance and placing them for analog. All of that, I think, can be captured inside of models.
Graham: It can be. The question is, how soon will it be efficient? We’ve spent a huge amount of time solving that problem deterministically, algorithmically, and mathematically so that we get the right answer every single time. What you’re proposing is, ‘Can we use a probabilistic model to solve those problems more efficiently?’ Today, ‘no’ is the very clear answer. With the speed of technological advancement, will that be compute-efficient and dollar-efficient in the next 2 years, 8 years, 10 years?
Thiruvengadam: I agree. The key point, again, is the march of nines. The march of nines will kick in, and you’ve got a 99.99999. You need to get 100% accuracy. We’re talking about subsuming two EDA tools into models.
Balasubramanian: That’s very important. In chip design, being 99.99% accurate is a failure. All it takes is one picosecond and you have a whole violation.
Petr: We keep forgetting that we still have not fully understood all the physics. Every single model we have is a simplification of the real world. It’s an error of an error of an error of an error. No matter how well you go on the whole agentic framework, at some point, there’s a trade-off somewhere. And if you don’t capture that, your chip is dead. We spent decades optimizing the simulator engines to get deterministic results. There’s always an argument in those AI frameworks, ‘Oh, just run reinforcement learning. It can do it.’ Fair, it can. But my mathematically based optimizer is still faster and more accurate. Why would I want to do that?
Thiruvengadam: It’s important to understand that the march of nines is a problem in software. Why would it not be a problem in hardware? In chip design, it’s even more of a problem. In software, they talk about getting 100%. Failure is an important part. In hardware, costs are so high that the march of nines becomes an even bigger problem.
Balasubramanian: As we go down the flow, the band of how much error you can tolerate drops drastically.
SE: In an orchestral multi-agentic flow, who has a kill switch to prevent agents from burning through tokens and trying forever to gain 100% coverage closure, for example?
Graham: This is part of the prep before you deploy, which must be part of the infrastructure. We all have infrastructure this must sit on — the guardrails. There are still infinite problems in IC design and verification. Fundamentally, it’s an infinite or near-infinite problem, so there must be guardrails somewhere on how much time, how many tokens, and what the tool covers, etc. One thing EDA has been good at over the years is having tool providers address that with customers, having customers understand the best ROI trade-offs, and pushing us to provide them. Up until now, it was cycles on a given problem. We get the number of CPU cycles we think we need to do, whether we get them in the cloud or on-prem or whatever, for one of the thousand tasks you have to do from RTL to GDS. Now we’re adding tokens to those, but we need the same guardrails. We know this. Our customers employ entire departments of people to optimize this exact problem.
Petr: Infinite loops are not new to us. Every mathematical problem has infinite loops. If you get into those trenches, we have solutions.
SE: What about IP ownership if you’re using an agent for a design that you sell to a customer, or they use your agent for their design, who owns what IP?
Balasubramanian: IP ownership is one of the biggest concerns I’m hearing about, both from our side as the tool provider and from the customer side. Yes, [agents] can write code, but the challenge is that all it takes is one copyrighted piece of code getting into your codebase, and if you don’t verify it, you’re going to get a loss. That’s one thing. Second, the most important thing is, I always tell people that any prompt you do, that’s your IQ. You’re doing your foundation, you’re using Claude Code, and you’re letting your designers do certain things. Their prompt will be, ‘This is how I’m going to be solving this routing problem. Can you do this?’ Your prompt is pretty much your IP. You’re telling some people the algorithm for how to do certain things, and there is a lot of talk about, ‘They’re not going to look at it.’ But every prompt is necessary to the LLM providers. If it goes outside of the air gap, it’s a problem. So IP protection is going to be very key. How do you expose code outside, especially source code? That’s going to be very key, and that’s a big concern coming up.
Petr: Another problem is that U.S. copyright does not allow us to copyright code that has been generated by an AI. That means every chip designed by an AI isn’t copyrightable.
Balasubramanian: Yes, because LLMs are not [copyrightable].
Thiruvengadam: The key distinction is that we are not talking about a chip that’s 100% designed by AI with no human intervention.
Petr: There’s a clause in the copyright that says the majority of the [design] has to be done by a human and, I’m sorry to say that, but the majority is not going to be.
Balistreri: I want to recap a bit and then get to this point. There are many problems, many layers of problems, with deploying AI in a high ROI way that organizations will accept meets their security requirements. One is cost. We solve that at the harness layer. The same model, doing like-for-like tasks, uses 40% fewer tokens. Our own model is open-weight and performs similarly, but at lower cost. Then there’s the full-flow problem, which is where you need the ontology. You can’t just do point acceleration. Then there’s the autonomous problem, which is the trust. Are there going to be critical errors? Are those gated and built into your system so you can’t produce things? Then there’s the IP and security issue, and it’s a pretty simple question. Do you want to send your inference over the public internet to a model provider that is building chips that compete with your chips? If you use frontier models in your agentic layer, whatever agents you use, you run that risk. Some don’t even have zero data retention. The clear answer to us — in a highly security-focused industry, where your design and design flow itself is IP — is that you need a solution with a custom model you can deploy on-prem. That also solves the IP question. I’m not a copyright lawyer, but if the design never leaves your environment, it’s de facto still yours. It’s not copyrighted per se, but no one else can access it.
Petr: Don’t underestimate reverse engineering.
Read parts one and two of the discussion:
Agentic AI Success Relies On Excellent Human Scaffolding
Before deploying agentic AI into a chip design, engineers must define the domain ontology and agentic harness. Fundamental engines are still crucial.
Token Costs Are Becoming The New EDA Budget Battle
Cost per token is causing EDA design budgets to balloon; what comes next isn’t entirely clear yet.

articles.title: Noch Super-Nintendo-Spiele im Schrank? Dann ist dieses Gadget für euch
articles.text:
Noch Super-Nintendo-Spiele im Schrank? Dann ist dieses Gadget für euch
So eine Retro-Spielesammlung kann auch ziemlich lästig sein. Nur mit teils umständlichen Stecksystemen oder kostspieligen Konvertern lassen sich die alten Konsolen noch an moderne Fernseher oder Monitore anschließen. Und dann stehen die klobigen Kisten auch gerne mal im Weg herum – wenn sie denn noch funktionieren.
Wer aber dennoch den Charme von alten Cartridges mag, womöglich sogar noch ein paar Spiele für das Super Nintendo Entertainment System (SNES) herumliegen hat, sollte einen Blick auf den SN Operator von Epilogue werfen. Der kann sogar deutlich mehr, als nur alte SNES-Games abzuspielen.
Alte Spiele auf modernen Rechnern
Bereits seit 2021 bietet Epilogue mit dem GB Operator eine Möglichkeit an, physische Spiele für Gameboy und Gameboy Advance auf Windows, macOS oder Linux zu spielen. Die Cartridges werden in das Gadget gesteckt, das wiederum per USB-C mit einem Rechner verbunden ist. Steuern könnt ihr die Games dann mit einem angeschlossenen Controller, oder einer Tastatur.
Doch das Gadget hat viele weitere nützliche Features, die auch im SN Operator enthalten sind. So könnt ihr etwa die Speicherstände eurer physischen SNES-Spiele (sowohl NTSC als auch PAL) digitalisieren und auf dem PC oder Mac speichern. Denn eine Schwachstelle der alten Cartridges sind oft die Batterien, die für die Sicherung der Speicherstände nötig sind.
Besonders für Sammler dürfte es interessant sein, dass der SN Operator auch gefälschte Spiele erkennen kann. Es kann schließlich immer wieder vorkommen, dass ihr gebrauchte Spiele auf einem Flohmarkt oder auf Ebay kauft – und gar nicht merkt, dass es sich nicht um Originale handelt. Schon der GB Operator hat eine Genauigkeit von 98,7 Prozent beim Erkennen von Fälschungen versprochen.
SNES-Spiele mit Achievements
Eine weitere Funktion spricht derweil Gamer an, die Statistiken mögen, oder Wert auf kompetitives Spielen legen. Durch eine Integration der Online-Plattform Retroachievements ist es möglich, Achievements für eure physischen SNES-Spiele zu erhalten, Bestzeiten mit Freunden zu vergleichen oder euren Fortschritt festzuhalten – so wie es auf modernen Systemen längst der Fall ist.
Solltet ihr zudem zu den wenigen Personen gehören, die die Light Gun Super Scope oder die SNES Mouse besitzen, hat der SN Operator auch dafür eine Lösung. So könnt ihr einfach eure normale Maus für diese Steuerungsmethoden nutzen.
Der SN Operator kostet 71,39 US-Dollar, umgerechnet um die 62 Euro. Hinzu kommen etwa 10 Euro Versandkosten nach Deutschland.
Dieser Artikel wurde ursprünglich am 30.12.2025 veröffentlicht, interessiert jedoch immer noch sehr viele unserer Leser:innen. Deshalb haben wir ihn aktualisiert und hier nochmals zur Verfügung gestellt.

articles.title: Sophie Adenot bientôt de retour sur Terre : pourquoi la gravité sera son plus grand défi
articles.text:
Trois sorties extravéhiculaires, dont une de près de 7 heures : depuis février 2026, le séjour de Sophie Adenot a déjà mis son corps à rude épreuve. Son retour sur Terre approche : même si la date exacte du départ de l’ISS de Sophie Adenot n’est pas encore fixée, on sait que l’équipage de Crew-13, qui prendra la relève, se prépare au décollage pour le 1er octobre 2026. La rotation entre les équipages ne devrait donc pas tarder à s’organiser, ce qui sera synonyme de fin de mission pour Sophie Adenot.
Même une fois la mission achevée, quand l’astronaute française sera de retour sur la terre ferme, elle ne sera pas au bout de ses peines. Après des mois en apesanteur, son organisme aura en quelque sorte désappris la gravité.
Là-haut, un corps qui se déconditionne
Dans la Station spatiale internationale, le corps ne porte plus son propre poids. On parle d’apesanteur, même si les scientifiques préfèrent le terme de microgravité : une gravité résiduelle subsiste toujours, mais le corps, lui, flotte. Ses muscles travaillent alors beaucoup moins, et ses os se déminéralisent peu à peu. C’est pour limiter cette perte osseuse que les astronautes font autant de sport en orbite, chaque jour.
De retour, tout pèse une tonne
La première sensation, à l’atterrissage, est souvent le poids de sa propre tête. L’astronaute français Thomas Pesquet a raconté cette impression troublante, comme si sa tête basculait toute seule. Chaque objet semble soudain peser une tonne, et le moindre geste peut donner la nausée.
À l’intérieur, c’est la pagaille. En orbite, le cœur envoie moins de sang vers le cerveau, car il n’a plus à lutter contre la pesanteur. De retour au sol, cette adaptation se retourne contre l’astronaute : les malaises et les évanouissements sont fréquents dans les premières heures.
Le cerveau, lui, est déboussolé. Il doit retrouver ses repères pour tenir en équilibre, s’orienter, distinguer le haut du bas. Autant d’informations que la gravité nous fournit en permanence, sans qu’on y prête attention.
Il y a aussi ce réflexe oublié : sur Terre, tout tombe. Thomas Marshburn, astronaute de la Nasa, en a fait une vidéo pleine d’humour, en lâchant une tasse et un stylo comme s’ils allaient flotter autour de lui. Ce réflexe met quelques jours à revenir. Pesquet, lui, s’était retrouvé fasciné par sa première douche, à regarder les gouttes tomber bien droit vers le bas.
Le corps des astronautes, un véritable laboratoire
Tous ces symptômes intéressent les scientifiques au plus haut point. Le corps des astronautes devient un laboratoire à lui seul : en le comparant avant et après la mission, les chercheurs mesurent comment l’organisme humain encaisse l’absence de gravité, puis s’y réadapte. Notre corps orchestre en permanence des mécanismes qu’on ne remarque même pas.
Pendant des mois, Sophie Adenot aura vécu sans presque aucune gravité. En rentrant, elle va redécouvrir la plus banale des sensations : le poids de son propre corps. Comme souvent dans l’aventure spatiale, il faut s’éloigner de la Terre pour comprendre à quel point notre organisme est réglé pour y vivre.
